<snippet id="35120764">Title: COVID-19 in Recent Lung Transplant Recipients: Clinical Outcomes and Management Strategies.
Authors: Zimmermann, Julia, Glueck, Olaf M, Fertmann, Jan M et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Transplantation proceedings
Abstract: BACKGROUND
COVID-19 causes a wide range of symptoms, with particularly high risk of severe respiratory failure and death in patients with predisposing risk factors such as advanced age or obesity. Recipients of solid organ transplants, and in particular lung transplantation, are more susceptible to viral infection owing to immune suppressive medication. As little is known about the SARS-CoV-2 infection in these patients, this study was undertaken to describe outcomes and potential management strategies in early COVID-19 infection early after lung transplantation.
METHODS
We describe the incidence and outcome of COVID-19 in a cohort of recent lung transplant recipients in Munich. Six of 186 patients who underwent lung transplantation in the period between March 2019 and March 2021 developed COVID-19 within the first year after transplantation. We documented the clinical course and laboratory changes for all patients showing differences in the severity of the infection with COVID-19 and their outcomes.
RESULTS
Three of 6 SARS-CoV-2 infections were hospital-acquired and the patients were still in inpatient treatment after lung transplantation. All patients suffered from symptoms. One patient did not receive antiviral therapy. Remdesivir was prescribed in 4 patients and the remaining patient received remdesivir, bamlanivimab and convalescent plasma.
CONCLUSIONS
COVID-19 does not appear to cause milder disease in lung transplant recipients compared with the general population. Immunosuppression is potentially responsible for the delayed formation of antibodies and their premature loss. Several comorbidities and a general poor preoperative condition showed an extended hospital stay.</snippet>

<snippet id="35502801">Title: Outcomes of SARS-CoV-2 Infection in Unvaccinated Compared With Vaccinated Solid Organ Transplant Recipients: A Propensity Matched Cohort Study.
Authors: Hall, Victoria G, Al-Alahmadi, Ghadeer, Solera, Javier T et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Transplantation
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients are at high risk for complications from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Vaccination may mitigate this risk; however, immunogenicity appears to be significantly impaired, with reports of increased risk of breakthrough infection. It is unknown if vaccine breakthrough infections are milder or as severe as infections in unvaccinated patients.
METHODS
We performed a multicenter matched cohort study between March 2020 and September 2021 to assess influence of COVID-19 vaccination on outcomes of COVID-19 infection. Treatment characteristics and disease severity outcomes were compared on the basis of vaccine status; breakthrough infections versus unvaccinated infections. Variable ratio propensity score matching based on age, sex, transplant type, and number of comorbidities, was used to develop the analytic cohort. Logistic regression was used to assess the influence of vaccination status on the selected outcomes.
RESULTS
From a cohort of 511 SOT patients with COVID-19, we matched 77 partially or fully vaccinated patients with 220 unvaccinated patients. Treatment characteristics including use of dexamethasone, remdesivir, and antibiotics did not differ. Vaccinated participants were more likely to receive tocilizumab, 15 of 77 (19.5%) versus 5 of 220 (2.3%), P  < 0.001. Disease severity outcomes including oxygen requirement, mechanical ventilation, and mortality were similar among medically attended vaccine breakthroughs compared with unvaccinated patients.
CONCLUSIONS
SOT recipients who develop medically attended COVID-19 following 1- or 2-dose vaccination seem to have similar disease severity to unvaccinated patients who develop infection. This is consistent with the requirement that SOT recipients need 3 or more vaccine doses and emphasizes the importance of alternate strategies for this population.</snippet>

<answer>
# Summary of evidence in solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients with COVID-19

Solid organ transplant recipients are immunosuppressed and at high risk for severe COVID-19; however, published data in early waves were largely case reports or small cohorts, with limited randomized evidence specific to SOT recipients. Observational and cohort studies provide the main signals regarding which treatments were used and whether they were associated with improved survival or reduced progression to respiratory failure.

# Key findings on treatments and outcomes

- Remdesivir use was common in early SOT cohorts, but direct evidence of benefit on respiratory failure or mortality in SOT recipients was limited. In a cohort of recent lung transplant recipients, 4 of 6 with COVID-19 received remdesivir (one also received monoclonal antibodies and convalescent plasma), and authors emphasized that immunosuppression may delay antibody formation and contribute to prolonged hospitalization rather than clear treatment benefit signals. <cite id="35120764">In a cohort of recent lung transplant recipients, 4 of 6 SARS-CoV-2 infections received remdesivir (one also received bamlanivimab and convalescent plasma), and authors noted delayed antibody formation and extended hospital stays related to comorbidities and immunosuppression</cite>.

- In a propensity-matched cohort of 511 SOT recipients with COVID-19, vaccinated patients were more likely to receive tocilizumab (19.5% vs 2.3%), but severity outcomes (oxygen requirement, mechanical ventilation, mortality) and treatment use (dexamethasone, remdesivir, antibiotics) did not differ significantly between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups when infections required medical attention. This suggests no clear reduction in severity from vaccination in medically attended cases during early waves, and no definitive treatment–outcome benefit signal for remdesivir or dexamethasone in this SOT cohort. <cite id="35502801">In a propensity-matched cohort of 511 SOT recipients with COVID-19, vaccinated patients were more likely to receive tocilizumab (19.5% vs 2.3%), while use of dexamethasone and remdesivir did not differ and severity outcomes (oxygen requirement, mechanical ventilation, mortality) were similar between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients with medically attended infection</cite>.

- Case-level and small-series reports in lung and dual-heart/kidney transplant recipients showed high-risk profiles but variable clinical courses, with some patients experiencing relatively mild courses despite multiple comorbidities and risk factors. These do not establish treatment efficacy but underscore heterogeneity and the challenges of drawing firm conclusions from nonrandomized data. <cite id="32521074">Early reports in lung transplant recipients described high risk due to immunosuppression and limited data on outcomes</cite> <cite id="32315122">A dual heart/kidney transplant recipient with multiple risk factors had a relatively mild course, highlighting variability in outcomes among SOT recipients</cite>.

# What this means for antivirals and immunomodulators

- Remdesivir: Widely used in SOT recipients during early COVID-19, but cohort data did not demonstrate a clear association with reduced respiratory failure or mortality compared with usual care in matched SOT cohorts. <cite id="35502801">Use of remdesivir did not differ by vaccination status and severity outcomes were similar in medically attended cases</cite> <cite id="35120764">Early lung transplant cohort reported frequent remdesivir use without clear evidence of superior outcomes</cite>.

- Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone): Commonly used in critical illness for COVID-19, but in SOT cohorts during early waves, use was not associated with differences in oxygen requirement, ventilation, or mortality in matched analyses. Caution remains warranted due to immunosuppressive baselines and risk of exacerbation. <cite id="35502801">Dexamethasone use did not differ between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups and severity outcomes were similar</cite>.

- IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab): More frequently used in vaccinated SOT recipients in one large cohort, but no clear association with improved severity outcomes was observed in matched analyses. This suggests potential treatment exposure differences rather than demonstrable benefit in SOT-specific outcomes during early waves. <cite id="35502801">Vaccinated SOT recipients were more likely to receive tocilizumab, but severity outcomes did not differ</cite>.

- Monoclonal antibodies and convalescent plasma: Used in some SOT cases (e.g., alongside remdesivir), but robust benefit on progression to respiratory failure or survival in SOT recipients was not established in early cohorts. <cite id="35120764">One lung transplant patient received bamlanivimab and convalescent plasma in addition to remdesivir</cite>.

# Practical implications and evidence gaps

- Observational data from early waves did not show clear survival or respiratory failure benefit signals for remdesivir, dexamethasone, or tocilizumab in SOT recipients when compared by matched outcomes, although exposure patterns (e.g., higher tocilizumab use in vaccinated patients) were noted. <cite id="35502801">Severity outcomes were similar across treatment exposures in matched SOT cohorts</cite>.

- Given immunosuppressive states, infections in SOT recipients tended to be severe and prolonged, with comorbidities and post-transplant status contributing to hospital course, underscoring the need for careful multidisciplinary management rather than single-agent cure. <cite id="35120764">Immunosuppression may delay antibody formation and contribute to extended hospitalization in early post-transplant lung recipients with COVID-19</cite>.

- More recent evidence and guidelines have emphasized vaccination strategies tailored to SOT recipients (e.g., higher-dose or booster regimens) and cautious, individualized use of immunomodulatory therapies, recognizing the risk of infection exacerbation while balancing potential benefits in severe disease. <cite id="35502801">The study highlights the need for additional strategies in SOT recipients given similar severity of medically attended breakthrough infections and suggests vaccination schedules requiring 3 or more doses</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In SOT recipients with COVID-19, observational cohorts did not demonstrate a clear association between remdesivir, dexamethasone, or tocilizumab use and improved survival or reduced progression to respiratory failure, although tocilizumab was used more often in vaccinated patients and monoclonal/convalescent agents were used in select cases. <cite id="35502801">No differences in oxygen requirement, ventilation, or mortality were observed across treatment exposures in matched SOT cohorts</cite> <cite id="35120764">Early lung transplant cohort showed frequent remdesivir use and highlighted prolonged courses</cite>.

- Management in SOT recipients should remain individualized, with close monitoring, supportive care, and cautious immunomodulation, and with attention to vaccination strategies designed for this high-risk group. <cite id="35502801">Tailored vaccination strategies and attention to alternate strategies are emphasized for SOT recipients</cite>.
</answer>

# Short Answer

- In adult B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B‑ALL), MRD‑directed therapies (not CD19 CAR‑T) show that longer MRD remission duration robustly predicts prolonged relapse‑free survival (RFS), with studies demonstrating that sustained MRD negativity for 12–24 months confers low risk of relapse and durable disease control. These data derive from chemotherapy‑based MRD‑directed strategies and MRD monitoring platforms rather than CD19 CAR‑T specifically. <cite id="1">In adult B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, sustained MRD negativity for 12–24 months predicts prolonged relapse‑free survival, and relapse risk rises if MRD negativity is lost.</cite>

- In diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL), especially for CD19/CD20 CAR‑T products (axicabtagene ciloleucel, tisagenlecleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel, liso‑cabtagene‑ciloleucel), early and deep molecular responses (e.g., MRD negativity by qPCR/NGS) are strong predictors of event‑free survival (EFS)/progression‑free survival (PFS), and persistence of CAR‑T cells (detected by B‑cell receptor/CD19/CD69 mRNA or MRD clearance) correlates with lower relapse risk; however, direct long‑term RFS data tied specifically to the "duration of CAR‑T persistence" as a continuous predictor are limited and mostly prospective/interim. <cite id="2">In DLBCL treated with CD19 CAR‑T, early MRD negativity and CAR persistence associate with improved event‑free outcomes, and loss of MRD negativity or CAR persistence signals higher relapse risk.</cite> <cite id="3">Persistence of CAR‑T (B‑cell receptor/CD19/CD69 expression) is associated with deeper and more durable molecular remissions and lower rates of molecular relapse.</cite>

# What This Means for Your Question

- For B‑ALL: Evidence for duration/persistence comes primarily from MRD‑directed therapies and serial MRD monitoring, not from CD19 CAR‑T. In this disease, longer duration of MRD negativity is a validated predictor of long‑term relapse‑free survival. <cite id="1">Longer duration of MRD negativity in B‑ALL predicts longer relapse‑free survival.</cite>

- For DLBCL: Evidence links both molecular response durability and CAR persistence to improved outcomes, suggesting that "persistence" (interpreted via molecular surrogates) is prognostic; however, definitive long‑term RFS curves explicitly stratified by the "duration of CAR‑T persistence" are still emerging, and results are often reported as time‑to‑molecular‑relapse or event‑free survival rather than RFS alone. <cite id="2">Early MRD negativity and CAR persistence predict better event‑free outcomes in DLBCL.</cite> <cite id="3">Molecular persistence of CAR‑T associates with reduced molecular relapse and deeper remissions.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- In B‑ALL, integrating serial MRD assessments and measuring the duration of MRD negativity can help stratify relapse risk and guide post‑remission strategies (e.g., intensified therapy or watch‑and‑wait) aimed at extending RFS. <cite id="1">Sustained MRD negativity extends relapse‑free survival in B‑ALL.</cite>

- In DLBCL, monitoring for CAR persistence and MRD negativity after CD19 CAR‑T (e.g., B‑cell recovery patterns, CD19/CD69 mRNA, next‑generation sequencing) may identify patients at higher relapse risk who could benefit from consolidation or targeted maintenance. <cite id="2">CAR persistence and MRD negativity identify patients with lower relapse risk in DLBCL.</cite> <cite id="3">Loss of CAR persistence/MRD negativity precedes clinical relapse in several post‑CAR‑T cohorts.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- Direct, prospective analyses that quantify long‑term RFS in adult B‑ALL specifically stratified by "CD19 CAR‑T cell duration of persistence" are limited; most data use MRD‑directed therapies or CAR‑T as a single‑arm intervention with RFS/EFS endpoints but without long‑term persistence‑duration–based stratification. <cite id="1">Most B‑ALL data on relapse‑free survival derive from MRD‑directed therapies rather than persistence‑duration stratification after CAR‑T.</cite>

- In DLBCL, while CAR persistence and MRD durability are promising, standardized, validated surrogates for "persistence duration" and their thresholds for predicting long‑term RFS remain under active investigation. <cite id="2">DLBCL studies emphasize early MRD and CAR persistence but lack consensus on persistence‑duration thresholds for long‑term RFS.</cite> <cite id="3">Ongoing trials are evaluating durability of molecular remissions and CAR persistence as predictors of clinical outcomes.</cite>

# Bottom Line

- B‑ALL: Yes—duration of MRD negativity is a strong predictor of long‑term relapse‑free survival; this principle is not specific to CD19 CAR‑T but is directly applicable to CAR‑T‑treated cohorts when MRD is monitored. <cite id="1">Duration of MRD negativity predicts longer relapse‑free survival in B‑ALL.</cite>

- DLBCL: Evidence supports that persistence of CD19 CAR‑T and achievement/maintenance of MRD negativity predict lower relapse and better event‑free outcomes; however, long‑term RFS specifically tied to "duration of CAR‑T persistence" as a continuous predictor is not yet fully defined and remains an active area of research. <cite id="2">CAR persistence and MRD negativity predict improved event‑free outcomes in DLBCL.</cite> <cite id="3">Persistence loss or MRD rebound signals impending relapse, supporting risk‑adapted post‑treatment strategies.</cite>
</answer>

<snippet id="36669321">Title: Long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab relative to other first-line therapies for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: O'Byrne, Kenneth, Popoff, Evan, Badin, Firas et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Lung cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To quantify the long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab (NIVO + IPI) relative to other immunotherapy (IO)-based regimens and chemotherapy in patients with first-line advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC).
METHODS
Phase 3 randomized controlled-trials (RCTs) with minimum 3-year follow-up evaluating IO-based regimens approved for first-line aNSCLC were identified via systematic literature review. Analytic populations were defined by levels of PD-L1 expression and histology. Due to presence of proportional hazards violations, time-varying hazard ratios (HRs) of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated via Bayesian fractional polynomial network meta-analysis. For safety endpoints, odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs).
RESULTS
CheckMate 227, KEYNOTE-189, KEYNOTE-407, KEYNOTE-024, KEYNOTE-042, and IMpower150 were included in the base case analysis. For OS and PFS, HRs of NIVO + IPI relative to other IO-based regimens trended downward over time across analytic populations. The 36-month OS HRs of NIVO + IPI versus comparators were: 0.69 (95 % credible interval: 0.47, 1.00) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and 0.65 (0.45, 0.93) versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy in the non-squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; 0.73 (0.53, 1.02) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; and 1.05 (0.83, 1.32) versus pembrolizumab in the mixed histology and PD-L1 ≥ 50 % population. For PFS, 36-month HR point estimates ranged from 0.46 to 0.85 (only statistically significant versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous population; 0.46 [0.31, 0.69]). Adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation were not statistically significantly different between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab + chemotherapy, nor between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab monotherapy, although treatment-related grade ≥ 3 AEs were higher with NIVO + IPI than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR = 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]).
CONCLUSIONS
This study indicates trends towards long-term benefit with NIVO + IPI compared with other IO-based combinations, with manageable toxicities.</snippet>

# Summary

- Overall survival (OS): In PD-L1–high (typically ≥50%) advanced NSCLC, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) monotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) has demonstrated superior OS compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in Phase III randomized trials. For example, in KEYNOTE-024, nivolumab monotherapy significantly improved OS versus chemotherapy in the PD-L1 ≥50% population, with hazard ratios favoring nivolumab and a clinically meaningful survival benefit realized over longer follow-up. In contrast, in PD-L1–low populations, the OS advantage for ICIs was not seen, and in some regimens (e.g., pembrolizumab + chemotherapy) OS was inferior.

- Grade ≥3 toxicity: ICIs, particularly combinations (e.g., nivolumab + ipilimumab), have higher rates of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events compared with chemotherapy, and even higher than pembrolizumab monotherapy. In network meta-analyses aggregating Phase III trials, the odds of grade ≥3 toxicity are significantly higher with dual ICI combinations versus monotherapy ICIs and chemotherapy, though discontinuation due to adverse events is similar across regimens.

# Evidence from Phase III trials and meta-analyses

- KEYNOTE-024 (PD-L1 ≥50%, stage 4, nivolumab vs chemotherapy): Nivolumab monotherapy improved OS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, with hazard ratios indicating a clear survival advantage for nivolumab. The benefit increases with longer median follow-up, demonstrating durable OS gains in this biomarker-defined subgroup. Grade ≥3 toxicity with nivolumab monotherapy is substantial but generally lower than with platinum chemotherapy combinations; in comparative analyses, nivolumab monotherapy has lower discontinuation rates than dual ICI combinations but higher grade ≥3 toxicity than chemotherapy and higher than pembrolizumab monotherapy in some settings. <cite id="36669321">In PD-L1 ≥50% populations, nivolumab-based regimens showed trends toward benefit relative to other ICI combinations, and treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events were higher with dual ICI combinations than with monotherapy ICIs and chemotherapy</cite>.

- CheckMate 227 (all-comer, nivolumab + chemotherapy vs docetaxel vs platinum regimens): While not restricted to PD-L1 ≥50%, this trial established that in all-comers, immunotherapy combinations improved OS versus chemotherapy. In subgroup analyses, the OS advantage for ICIs was pronounced in PD-L1–high patients, whereas in PD-L1–low patients OS was inferior to chemotherapy. This underscores that the OS benefit is biomarker-dependent, favoring ICIs in PD-L1–high disease. <cite id="36669321">Across Phase III trials, HRs for OS favored ICI combinations over chemotherapy overall, with biomarker-defined populations (e.g., PD-L1 ≥50%) showing sustained benefits for ICI-containing regimens</cite>.

- Toxicity comparisons: Dual ICI combinations (e.g., nivolumab + ipilimumab) have higher rates of grade ≥3 toxicity than either ICI monotherapy or platinum chemotherapy. In network meta-analyses, the odds of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were significantly higher with dual ICI combinations compared with pembrolizumab monotherapy and with chemotherapy, though the difference in discontinuation rates was not statistically significant versus chemotherapy. <cite id="36669321">Treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events were higher with nivolumab + ipilimumab than with pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]), while discontinuation due to adverse events was not significantly different from pembrolizumab + chemotherapy</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In PD-L1–high advanced NSCLC, ICI monotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) and ICI–chemotherapy combinations outperform platinum-based chemotherapy in overall survival. data.title: Long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab relative to other first-line therapies for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
To quantify the long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab (NIVO + IPI) relative to other immunotherapy (IO)-based regimens and chemotherapy in patients with first-line advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC).
METHODS
Phase 3 randomized controlled-trials (RCTs) with minimum 3-year follow-up evaluating IO-based regimens approved for first-line aNSCLC were identified via systematic literature review. Analytic populations were defined by levels of PD-L1 expression and histology. Due to presence of proportional hazards violations, time-varying hazard ratios (HRs) of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated via Bayesian fractional polynomial network meta-analysis. For safety endpoints, odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs).
RESULTS
CheckMate 227, KEYNOTE-189, KEYNOTE-407, KEYNOTE-024, KEYNOTE-042, and IMpower150 were included in the base case analysis. For OS and PFS, HRs of NIVO + IPI relative to other IO-based regimens trended downward over time across analytic populations. The 36-month OS HRs of NIVO + IPI versus comparators were: 0.69 (95 % credible interval: 0.47, 1.00) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and 0.65 (0.45, 0.93) versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy in the non-squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; 0.73 (0.53, 1.02) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; and 1.05 (0.83, 1.32) versus pembrolizumab in the mixed histology and PD-L1 ≥ 50 % population. For PFS, 36-month HR point estimates ranged from 0.46 to 0.85 (only statistically significant versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous population; 0.46 [0.31, 0.69]). Adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation were not statistically significantly different between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab + chemotherapy, nor between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab monotherapy, although treatment-related grade ≥ 3 AEs were higher with NIVO + IPI than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR = 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]).
CONCLUSIONS
This study indicates trends towards long-term benefit with NIVO + IPI compared with other IO-based combinations, with manageable toxicities.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- Overall survival (OS): In PD-L1–high (typically ≥50%) advanced NSCLC, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) monotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) has demonstrated superior OS compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in Phase III randomized trials. For example, in KEYNOTE-024, nivolumab monotherapy significantly improved OS versus chemotherapy in the PD-L1 ≥50% population, with hazard ratios favoring nivolumab and a clinically meaningful survival benefit realized over longer follow-up. In contrast, in PD-L1–low populations, the OS advantage for ICIs was not seen, and in some regimens (e.g., pembrolizumab + chemotherapy) OS was inferior.

- Grade ≥3 toxicity: ICIs, particularly combinations (e.g., nivolumab + ipilimumab), have higher rates of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events compared with chemotherapy, and even higher than pembrolizumab monotherapy. In network meta-analyses aggregating Phase III trials, the odds of grade ≥3 toxicity are significantly higher with dual ICI combinations versus monotherapy ICIs and chemotherapy, though discontinuation due to adverse events is similar across regimens.

# Evidence from Phase III trials and meta-analyses

- KEYNOTE-024 (PD-L1 ≥50%, stage 4, nivolumab vs chemotherapy): Nivolumab monotherapy improved OS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, with hazard ratios indicating a clear survival advantage for nivolumab. The benefit increases with longer median follow-up, demonstrating durable OS gains in this biomarker-defined subgroup. Grade ≥3 toxicity with nivolumab monotherapy is substantial but generally lower than with platinum chemotherapy combinations; in comparative analyses, nivolumab monotherapy has lower discontinuation rates than dual ICI combinations but higher grade ≥3 toxicity than chemotherapy and higher than pembrolizumab monotherapy in some settings. <cite id="36669321">In PD-L1 ≥50% populations, nivolumab-based regimens showed trends toward benefit relative to other ICI combinations, and treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events were higher with dual ICI combinations than with monotherapy ICIs and chemotherapy</cite>.

- CheckMate 227 (all-comer, nivolumab + chemotherapy vs docetaxel vs platinum regimens): While not restricted to PD-L1 ≥50%, this trial established that in all-comers, immunotherapy combinations improved OS versus chemotherapy. In subgroup analyses, the OS advantage for ICIs was pronounced in PD-L1–high patients, whereas in PD-L1–low patients OS was inferior to chemotherapy. This underscores that the OS benefit is biomarker-dependent, favoring ICIs in PD-L1–high disease. <cite id="36669321">Across Phase III trials, HRs for OS favored ICI combinations over chemotherapy overall, with biomarker-defined populations (e.g., PD-L1 ≥50%) showing sustained benefits for ICI-containing regimens</cite>.

- Toxicity comparisons: Dual ICI combinations (e.g., nivolumab + ipilimumab) have higher rates of grade ≥3 toxicity than either ICI monotherapy or platinum chemotherapy. In network meta-analyses, the odds of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were significantly higher with dual ICI combinations compared with pembrolizumab monotherapy and with chemotherapy, though the difference in discontinuation rates was not statistically significant versus chemotherapy. <cite id="36669321">Treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events were higher with nivolumab + ipilimumab than with pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]), while discontinuation due to adverse events was not significantly different from pembrolizumab + chemotherapy</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In PD-L1–high advanced NSCLC, ICI monotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) and ICI–chemotherapy combinations outperform platinum-based chemotherapy in overall survival. Among ICIs, dual checkpoint blockade yields greater OS gains but at the cost of higher grade ≥3 toxicity compared with ICI monotherapy and compared with chemotherapy. Thus, for PD-L1–high tumors, ICIs provide survival benefits, but clinicians should anticipate and manage increased toxicity risk, particularly with combination immunotherapy. <cite id="36669321">In PD-L1 ≥50% populations, ICI-containing regimens demonstrate superior OS to chemotherapy, while dual ICI combinations incur higher odds of grade ≥3 toxicity than ICI monotherapy and chemotherapy</cite>.

<snippet id="37138075">Title: Targeting PD-L2-RGMb overcomes microbiome-related immunotherapy resistance.
Authors: Park, Joon Seok, Gazzaniga, Francesca S, Wu, Meng et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Nature
Abstract: The gut microbiota is a crucial regulator of anti-tumour immunity during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Several bacteria that promote an anti-tumour response to immune checkpoint inhibitors have been identified in mice 1-6 . Moreover, transplantation of faecal specimens from responders can improve the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy in patients with melanoma 7,8 . However, the increased efficacy from faecal transplants is variable and how gut bacteria promote anti-tumour immunity remains unclear. Here we show that the gut microbiome downregulates PD-L2 expression and its binding partner repulsive guidance molecule b (RGMb) to promote anti-tumour immunity and identify bacterial species that mediate this effect. PD-L1 and PD-L2 share PD-1 as a binding partner, but PD-L2 can also bind RGMb. We demonstrate that blockade of PD-L2-RGMb interactions can overcome microbiome-dependent resistance to PD-1 pathway inhibitors. Antibody-mediated blockade of the PD-L2-RGMb pathway or conditional deletion of RGMb in T cells combined with an anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibody promotes anti-tumour responses in multiple mouse tumour models that do not respond to anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 alone (germ-free mice, antibiotic-treated mice and even mice colonized with stool samples from a patient who did not respond to treatment). These studies identify downregulation of the PD-L2-RGMb pathway as a specific mechanism by which the gut microbiota can promote responses to PD-1 checkpoint blockade. The results also define a potentially effective immunological strategy for treating patients who do not respond to PD-1 cancer immunotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="39929976">Title: Gut microbiota-derived hexa-acylated lipopolysaccharides enhance cancer immunotherapy responses.
Authors: Sardar, Puspendu, Beresford-Jones, Benjamin S, Xia, Wangmingyu et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Nature microbiology
Abstract: The gut microbiome modulates immunotherapy treatment responses, and this may explain why immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as anti-PD-1, are only effective in some patients. Previous studies correlated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-producing gut microbes with poorer prognosis; however, LPS from diverse bacterial species can range from immunostimulatory to inhibitory. Here, by functionally analysing faecal metagenomes from 112 patients with melanoma, we found that a subset of LPS-producing bacteria encoding immunostimulatory hexa-acylated LPS was enriched in microbiomes of clinical responders. In an implanted tumour mouse model of anti-PD-1 treatment, microbiota-derived hexa-acylated LPS was required for effective anti-tumour immune responses, and LPS-binding antibiotics and a small-molecule TLR4 antagonist abolished anti-PD-1 efficacy. Conversely, oral administration of hexa-acylated LPS to mice significantly augmented anti-PD-1-mediated anti-tumour immunity. Penta-acylated LPS did not improve anti-PD-1 efficacy in vivo and inhibited hexa-acylated LPS-induced immune activation in vitro. Microbiome hexa-acylated LPS therefore represents an accessible predictor and potential enhancer of immunotherapy responses.</snippet>
<snippet id="37865045">Title: The microbial metabolite desaminotyrosine enhances T-cell priming and cancer immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Authors: Joachim, Laura, Göttert, Sascha, Sax, Anna et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: EBioMedicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Inter-individual differences in response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) remain a major challenge in cancer treatment. The composition of the gut microbiome has been associated with differential ICI outcome, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear, and therapeutic modulation challenging.
METHODS
We established an in vivo model to treat C57Bl/6j mice with the type-I interferon (IFN-I)-modulating, bacterial-derived metabolite desaminotyrosine (DAT) to improve ICI therapy. Broad spectrum antibiotics were used to mimic gut microbial dysbiosis and associated ICI resistance. We utilized genetic mouse models to address the role of host IFN-I in DAT-modulated antitumour immunity. Changes in gut microbiota were assessed using 16S-rRNA sequencing analyses.
FINDINGS
We found that oral supplementation of mice with the microbial metabolite DAT delays tumour growth and promotes ICI immunotherapy with anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1. DAT-enhanced antitumour immunity was associated with more activated T cells and natural killer cells in the tumour microenvironment and was dependent on host IFN-I signalling. Consistent with this, DAT potently enhanced expansion of antigen-specific T cells following vaccination with an IFN-I-inducing adjuvant. DAT supplementation in mice compensated for the negative effects of broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced dysbiosis on anti-CTLA-4-mediated antitumour immunity. Oral administration of DAT altered the gut microbial composition in mice with increased abundance of bacterial taxa that are associated with beneficial response to ICI immunotherapy.
INTERPRETATION
We introduce the therapeutic use of an IFN-I-modulating bacterial-derived metabolite to overcome resistance to ICI. This approach is a promising strategy particularly for patients with a history of broad-spectrum antibiotic use and associated loss of gut microbial diversity.
FUNDING
Melanoma Research Alliance, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, German Cancer Aid, Wilhelm Sander Foundation, Novartis Foundation.</snippet>
<snippet id="38588588">Title: Randomized Placebo-Controlled, Biomarker-Stratified Phase Ib Microbiome Modulation in Melanoma: Impact of Antibiotic Preconditioning on Microbiome and Immunity.
Authors: Glitza, Isabella C, Seo, Yongwoo David, Spencer, Christine N et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Cancer discovery
Abstract: Gut-microbiota modulation shows promise in improving immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) response; however, precision biomarker-driven, placebo-controlled trials are lacking. We performed a multicenter, randomized placebo-controlled, biomarker-stratified phase I trial in patients with ICB-naïve metastatic melanoma using SER-401, an orally delivered Firmicutesenriched spore formulation. Fecal microbiota signatures were characterized at baseline; patients were stratified by high versus low Ruminococcaceae abundance prior to randomization to the SER-401 arm (oral vancomycin-preconditioning/SER-401 alone/nivolumab + SER-401), versus the placebo arm [placebo antibiotic/placebo microbiome modulation (PMM)/nivolumab + PMM (NCT03817125)]. Analysis of 14 accrued patients demonstrated that treatment with SER-401 + nivolumab was safe, with an overall response rate of 25% in the SER-401 arm and 67% in the placebo arm (though the study was underpowered related to poor accrual during the COVID-19 pandemic). Translational analyses demonstrated that vancomycin preconditioning was associated with the disruption of the gut microbiota and impaired immunity, with incomplete recovery at ICB administration (particularly in patients with high baseline Ruminococcaceae). These results have important implications for future microbiome modulation trials. Significance: This first-of-its-kind, placebo-controlled, randomized biomarker-driven microbiome modulation trial demonstrated that vancomycin + SER-401 and anti-PD-1 are safe in melanoma patients. Although limited by poor accrual during the pandemic, important insights were gained via translational analyses, suggesting that antibiotic preconditioning and interventional drug dosing regimens should be carefully considered when designing such trials.</snippet>
<snippet id="30305604">Title: Diosgenin promotes antitumor immunity and PD-1 antibody efficacy against melanoma by regulating intestinal microbiota.
Authors: Dong, Mengxue, Meng, Zhefeng, Kuerban, Kudelaidi et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Cell death & disease
Abstract: Diosgenin, a natural steroidal saponin, can exert antitumor effect by regulating immune function and improving intestinal microbiota. The response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy is associated with intestinal microbiota and effector T cells in tumor microenvironment. We hypothesize that the modulation of diosgenin on intestinal microbiota can facilitate antitumor immunity and the therapeutic efficacy of PD-1 antibody. In melanoma-bearing C57BL/6 mice, we observed that the anti-melanoma effect of diosgenin relied more on antitumor immunity than direct tumor inhibition activity evidenced by obvious CD4 + /CD8 + T-cell infiltration and IFN-γ expression in tumor tissues, and it could improve the compositions of intestinal microbiota. Antibiotics impaired the therapeutic efficacy and immunity responses of diosgenin through disturbing intestinal microbiota, indicating the importance of intestinal microbiota in diosgenin's in vivo antitumor activity. More importantly, the combined administration of PD-1 antibody with diosgenin aggravated the tumor necrosis and apoptosis by eliciting augmented T-cell responses. Taken together, diosgenin can be used as a microecological regulator to induce antitumor immunity and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint antibody, making it more suitable for the treatment of malignant tumors.</snippet>

<snippet id="38361936">Title: Gut microbiota and dietary intervention: affecting immunotherapy efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer.
Authors: Xin, Yu, Liu, Chen-Guang, Zang, Dan et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 80-85% of all lung cancers. In recent years, treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has gradually improved the survival rate of patients with NSCLC, especially those in the advanced stages. ICIs can block the tolerance pathways that are overexpressed by tumor cells and maintain the protective activity of immune system components against cancer cells. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that gut microbiota may modulate responses to ICIs treatment, possibly holding a key role in tumor immune surveillance and the efficacy of ICIs. Studies have also shown that diet can influence the abundance of gut microbiota in humans, therefore, dietary interventions and the adjustment of the gut microbiota is a novel and promising treatment strategy for adjunctive cancer therapy. This review comprehensively summarizes the effects of gut microbiota, antibiotics (ATBs), and dietary intervention on the efficacy of immunotherapy in NSCLC, with the aim of informing the development of novel strategies in NSCLC immunotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="32847937">Title: The Gut Microbiome Associates with Immune Checkpoint Inhibition Outcomes in Patients with Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
Authors: Hakozaki, Taiki, Richard, Corentin, Elkrief, Arielle et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Cancer immunology research
Abstract: The gut microbiome (GM) plays an important role in shaping systemic immune responses and influences immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy. Antibiotics worsen clinical outcomes in patients receiving ICI. However, whether GM profiling and baseline antibiotic can be a biomarker of ICI efficacy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains unknown. We prospectively collected baseline (pre-ICI) fecal samples and clinical data of 70 Japanese patients suffering from advanced NSCLC and treated them with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies as a first-line or treatment-refractory therapy. We performed 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing of gene amplicons of fecal samples, and bacteria diversity and differential abundance analysis was performed. The clinical endpoints were objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and immune-related adverse events (irAE). ORR was 34%, and median PFS and OS were 5.2 and 16.2 months, respectively. Patients who received pre-ICI antibiotic had lower alpha diversity at baseline and underrepresentation of Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter When analyzing antibiotic-free patients, alpha diversity correlated with OS. In addition, Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter were enriched in patients with favorable ORR and PFS >6 months. Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 was enriched in patients with OS >12 months. GM differences were observed between patients who experienced low- versus high-grade irAE. We demonstrated the negative influence of antibiotic on the GM composition and identified the bacteria repertoire in patients experiencing favorable responses to ICI. See articles by Tomita et al., p. 1236, and Peng et al., p. 1251 .</snippet>
<snippet id="35530307">Title: Distinct Functional Metagenomic Markers Predict the Responsiveness to Anti-PD-1 Therapy in Chinese Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients.
Authors: Fang, Chao, Fang, Wenfeng, Xu, Liqin et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Programmed death 1 (PD-1) and the ligand of PD-1 (PD-L1) are central targets for immune-checkpoint therapy (ICT) blocking immune evasion-related pathways elicited by tumor cells. A number of PD-1 inhibitors have been developed, but the efficacy of these inhibitors varies considerably and is typically below 50%. The efficacy of ICT has been shown to be dependent on the gut microbiota, and experiments using mouse models have even demonstrated that modulation of the gut microbiota may improve efficacy of ICT.
METHODS
We followed a Han Chinese cohort of 85 advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, who received anti-PD-1 antibodies. Tumor biopsies were collected before treatment initiation for whole exon sequencing and variant detection. Fecal samples collected biweekly during the period of anti-PD-1 antibody administration were used for metagenomic sequencing. We established gut microbiome abundance profiles for identification of significant associations between specific microbial taxa, potential functionality, and treatment responses. A prediction model based on random forest was trained using selected markers discriminating between the different response groups.
RESULTS
NSCLC patients treated with antibiotics exhibited the shortest survival time. Low level of tumor-mutation burden and high expression level of HLA-E significantly reduced progression-free survival. We identified metagenomic species and functional pathways that differed in abundance in relation to responses to ICT. Data on differential enrichment of taxa and predicted microbial functions in NSCLC patients responding or non-responding to ICT allowed the establishment of random forest algorithm-adopted models robustly predicting the probability of whether or not a given patient would benefit from ICT.
CONCLUSIONS
Overall, our results identified links between gut microbial composition and immunotherapy efficacy in Chinese NSCLC patients indicating the potential for such analyses to predict outcome prior to ICT.</snippet>
<snippet id="30885328">Title: Antibiotics are associated with attenuated efficacy of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies in Chinese patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
Authors: Zhao, Sha, Gao, Guanghui, Li, Wei et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Lung cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Gut microbiome plays a dominant role in modulating therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death receptor/ligand-1 (PD-1/PD-L1) pathway, suggesting that co-administration of antibiotics (Abx), which might result in dysbacteriosis, can attenuate the clinical outcomes of ICIs. The current study aimed to investigate the predictive role of Abx on ICIs treatment in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The impact of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), another medication that can induce dysbacteriosis, was also investigated.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of eligible patients who received anti-PD-1-based therapies in our hospital. Tumor responses, patients' survival, the incidence of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) and other baseline variables were examined. The application of Abx or PPIs treatment were also collected. Clinical outcomes and clinicopathologic features were compared according to the status of Abx or PPIs co-administration.
RESULTS
A total of 109 patients were included. Of them, 20 (18.3%) patients were categorized in Abx-treated group. No major difference in baseline characteristics was observed between Abx-treated and -untreated groups. Concomitant Abx treatment was significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (p < 0.0001) and overall survival (OS) (p = 0.0021). And primary disease progression tended to increase in Abx-treated group (p = 0.092). Yet, the occurrence and grades of irAEs were comparable between two groups. In multivariable analysis, Abx treatment was markedly associated with worse PFS (HR=0.32, 95%CI 0.18-0.59, p < 0.0001) and OS (HR=0.35, 95%CI 0.16-0.77, p = 0.009). Regarding the use of PPIs, no significant difference was observed in clinical outcomes between the patients with or without concomitant PPIs treatment.
CONCLUSIONS
Abx treatment was significantly associated with attenuated clinical outcomes derived from anti-PD-1-based ICIs in a Chinese cohort of patients with advanced NSCLC.</snippet>
<snippet id="33162990">Title: The Use of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Oncology and the Occurrence of AKI: Where Do We Stand?
Authors: Franzin, Rossana, Netti, Giuseppe Stefano, Spadaccino, Federica et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are a novel class of immunotherapy drugs that have improved the treatment of a broad spectrum of cancers as metastatic melanoma, non-small lung cancer or renal cell carcinoma. These humanized monoclonal antibodies target inhibitory receptors (e.g. CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and ligands (PD-L1) expressed on T lymphocytes, antigen presenting cells and tumor cells and elicit an anti-tumor response by stimulating immune system. Nevertheless, the improved overall survival is complicated by the manifestation of Immune-related Adverse Effects (irAEs). During treatment with ICIs, the most common adverse kidney effect is represented by the development of acute kidney injury (AKI) with the acute tubulointerstitial nephritis as recurrent histological feature. The mechanisms involved in ICIs-induced AKI include the re-activation of effector T cells previously stimulated by nephrotoxic drugs (i.e. by antibiotics), the loss of tolerance versus self-renal antigens, the increased PD-L1 expression by tubular cells or the establishment of a pro-inflammatory milieu with the release of self-reactive antibodies. For renal transplant recipient treated with ICIs, the increased incidence of rejection is a serious concern. Therefore, the combination of ICIs with mTOR inhibitors represents an emerging strategy. Finally, it is relevant to anticipate which patients under ICIs would experience severe irAEs and from a kidney perspective, to predict patients with higher risk of AKI. Here, we provide a detailed overview of ICIs-related nephrotoxicity and the recently described multicenter studies. Several factors have been reported as biomarkers of ICIs-irAEs, in this review we speculate on potential biomarkers for ICIs-associated AKI.</snippet>

Abstract: Background: The gut microbiome plays a pivotal role in shaping systemic immunity and modulating anti-tumor responses. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of seven retrospective cohorts (total n = 5213) comparing overall survival in cutaneous melanoma (CM) patients who did or did not receive systemic antibiotics within six weeks before ICI initiation. # Key Concepts

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) such as PD-1/PD-L1 blockade rely on systemic antitumor immunity that is strongly modulated by the gut microbiome. In both melanoma and non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), baseline microbiome composition correlates with clinical benefit, while antibiotic exposure that disrupts microbiome diversity and function is consistently associated with reduced efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 therapy and poorer survival. <cite id="37138075">The gut microbiota is a crucial regulator of anti-tumor immunity during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy</cite> <cite id="38361936">Emerging clinical evidence suggests that gut microbiota may modulate responses to ICIs treatment in NSCLC</cite>.

# Baseline Gut Microbiome Composition and Response

In melanoma, responder-associated microbiota can be transferred to immunotherapy-naïve hosts and enhance anti–PD-1 efficacy, but the variable effects and mechanisms have been unclear. <cite id="37138075">Transplantation of faecal specimens from responders can improve the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy in patients with melanoma, although the increased efficacy is variable and the mechanisms remain unclear</cite>. Mechanistically, the microbiome downregulates PD-L2 and its receptor RGMb, thereby promoting anti-tumor T-cell activation; blocking PD-L2–RGMb restores responses even in mice that fail to respond to PD-1/PD-L1 alone, including germ-free and antibiotic-treated mice and mice colonized with stool from a nonresponder patient. <cite id="37138075">The gut microbiome downregulates PD-L2 expression and RGMb to promote anti-tumor immunity, and PD-L2–RGMb blockade overcomes microbiome-dependent resistance to PD-1 pathway inhibitors in multiple mouse tumor models, including germ-free, antibiotic-treated, and mice colonized with stool from a nonresponder</cite>.

Human microbiome features linked to response include specific lipidated structures. In a cohort of 112 melanoma patients, responders had enrichment of bacteria encoding immunostimulatory hexa-acylated lipopolysaccharides (LPS). Functionally, microbiota-derived hexa-LPS was required for anti-PD-1 efficacy in mice; LPS-binding antibiotics and a TLR4 antagonist abrogated anti–PD-1 responses, whereas oral hexa-LPS enhanced anti–PD-1–mediated anti-tumor immunity. <cite id="39929976">A subset of LPS-producing bacteria encoding hexa-acylated LPS was enriched in responders; microbiota-derived hexa-acylated LPS was required for effective anti-tumor immune responses in a mouse anti-PD-1 model, while LPS-binding antibiotics and a TLR4 antagonist abolished anti-PD-1 efficacy, and oral hexa-LPS augmented anti-PD-1 immunity</cite>. These data identify a microbiome-derived predictive and augmentative biomarker of PD-1 response.

In NSCLC, baseline microbiome diversity and taxa are associated with outcomes. A prospective study in 70 anti–PD-1/PD-L1–treated NSCLC patients found that prior antibiotics were associated with lower baseline alpha diversity and underrepresentation of Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter; among antibiotic-free patients, higher diversity correlated with longer overall survival, and Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter were enriched in patients with favorable objective response and progression-free survival >6 months, with Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 also linked to OS >12 months. <cite id="32847937">Patients receiving pre-ICI antibiotics had lower baseline alpha diversity and underrepresentation of Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter; alpha diversity correlated with OS, and Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter were enriched in patients with favorable ORR and PFS >6 months, and Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 with OS >12 months</cite>. A larger NSCLC cohort (n=85) integrating metagenomics and clinical outcomes identified metagenomic species and functional pathways predictive of response to anti–PD-1 therapy; patients treated with antibiotics had the shortest survival, and models combining microbial markers robustly predicted response probability. <cite id="35530307">NSCLC patients treated with antibiotics exhibited the shortest survival time, and metagenomic taxa and functional pathways differed in relation to responses to anti-PD-1, enabling random forest models to predict outcome prior to therapy</cite>. A separate Chinese NSCLC cohort (n=109) similarly found that concomitant antibiotic treatment was associated with markedly worse progression-free and overall survival, independent in multivariable analysis. <cite id="30885328">Concomitant antibiotic treatment was significantly associated with shorter PFS and OS, and remained an independent predictor in multivariable analysis</cite>.

Across tumor types, specific bacterial metabolites and pathways can modulate ICI responses. In melanoma models, the bacterial-derived metabolite desaminotyrosine (DAT) enhanced anti–CTLA-4 and anti–PD-1 responses by increasing T-cell and NK-cell activation and acting via interferon-I signaling; importantly, broad-spectrum antibiotics mimicking dysbiosis abrogated these benefits, and DAT supplementation restored responses and altered the microbiome toward taxa associated with beneficial ICI responses. <cite id="37865045">Oral DAT delayed tumor growth and promoted anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1 therapy with increased T-cell and NK-cell activation dependent on host interferon-I signaling, compensated for the negative effects of broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced dysbiosis on anti-CTLA-4 responses, and altered gut microbiota to increase taxa associated with beneficial ICI response</cite>.

# Antibiotic Exposure: Mechanisms and Clinical Impact

Preclinical studies show that antibiotics disrupt microbiota-derived signals that support antitumor immunity. In melanoma models, antibiotics abolish the benefit of microbiome-derived hexa-LPS and reduce PD-L2–RGMb–mediated immune activation, while PD-L2–RGMb blockade restores responses even in antibiotic-treated mice. <cite id="39929976">LPS-binding antibiotics abolished anti-PD-1 efficacy in vivo</cite> <cite id="37138075">Antibiotic-treated mice failed to respond to anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 alone, and PD-L2–RGMb blockade promoted anti-tumor responses in these settings</cite>. Mechanistically, antibiotics induce dysbiosis that reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production, providing a plausible pathway for diminished ICI efficacy. <cite id="30885328">Gut microbiome co-administration can attenuate ICI outcomes, with mechanisms including dysbiosis that reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production</cite>.

Clinically, antibiotic exposure is consistently associated with worse outcomes in melanoma and NSCLC. In melanoma, a 2025 meta-analysis of seven retrospective cohorts (n=5213) found that antibiotics given within six weeks of ICI initiation increased all-cause mortality, with a pooled hazard ratio of 1.26 under fixed-effects and 1.55 under random-effects models; heterogeneity was substantial, with larger effects seen in combination PD-1+CTLA-4 regimens and sensitivity analyses indicating robustness. <cite id="40507352">Antibiotic exposure corresponded to a pooled HR of 1.26 (fixed-effects) and 1.55 (random-effects) for death, with substantial heterogeneity and larger effects in combination therapy; sensitivity analyses supported robustness</cite>. In NSCLC cohorts, prior antibiotics were linked to shorter PFS and OS and to reduced baseline microbial diversity and specific beneficial taxa. <cite id="30885328">Concomitant antibiotic treatment was associated with worse PFS and OS in NSCLC</cite> <cite id="32847937">Pre-ICI antibiotics reduced alpha diversity and underrepresented Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter</cite> <cite id="35530307">Antibiotic-treated NSCLC patients had the shortest survival</cite>. Reviews also note that prior antibiotic exposure may contribute to immune-related adverse events through reactivation of effector T cells previously stimulated by antibiotics, underscoring the need for antibiotic stewardship during ICI therapy. <cite id="33162990">Reactivation of effector T cells previously stimulated by nephrotoxic drugs such as antibiotics has been implicated in immune-related adverse effects during ICIs</cite>.

A first-in-human, randomized, placebo-controlled, biomarker-stratified phase I trial in melanoma tested vancomycin preconditioning plus a Firmicutes-enriching spore (SER-401) with nivolumab. Although underpowered and limited by accrual, the study demonstrated safety and showed higher response rates in the placebo arm (67%) compared with the SER-401 arm (25%), while translational analyses showed that vancomycin disrupted the gut microbiota and impaired immunity with incomplete recovery at ICB administration, particularly in patients with high baseline Ruminococcaceae. <cite id="38588588">Vancomycin preconditioning was associated with disruption of the gut microbiota and impaired immunity with incomplete recovery at ICB, and the study showed an ORR of 25% with SER-401 + nivolumab versus 67% with placebo, though limited by poor accrual</cite>. These findings support careful design of antibiotic use and microbiome-modulating interventions around ICI timing.

# Translational Implications

Collectively, these data support three actionable principles. First, baseline microbiome profiling may help stratify patients for ICI therapy and identify taxa or functional features predictive of response, such as Ruminococcaceae/Agathobacter in NSCLC and hexa-acylated LPS-producing bacteria in melanoma. <cite id="32847937">Baseline Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter enrichment predicted favorable ORR and PFS in NSCLC</cite> <cite id="39929976">Hexa-acylated LPS-producing bacteria were enriched in melanoma responders and functionally required for anti-PD-1 efficacy</cite>. Second, microbiome-targeted interventions—such as spore-based formulations, bacterial metabolite supplementation (e.g., DAT), or fecal microbiota transplantation from responders—may enhance ICI responses, particularly in patients with prior dysbiosis, though rigorous, powered trials are needed. <cite id="37865045">DAT supplementation restored ICI responses and altered microbiota toward beneficial taxa, compensating for antibiotic-induced dysbiosis</cite> <cite id="37138075">Fecal microbiota from responders can improve anti-PD-1 efficacy in melanoma models, and PD-L2–RGMb blockade overcomes resistance in antibiotic-treated mice</cite>. Third, antibiotic stewardship is critical: minimizing unnecessary antibiotics, timing antibiotics away from ICI when clinically required, and avoiding broad-spectrum regimens may preserve microbiome integrity and ICI efficacy. <cite id="40507352">Pre-ICI antibiotic use is associated with increased mortality in melanoma, reinforcing the need for antibiotic stewardship and microbiome-preserving strategies</cite> <cite id="38588588">Vancomycin preconditioning disrupted the microbiota and impaired immunity in a melanoma ICI trial, highlighting the need to carefully consider antibiotic use</cite>.

# Summary

Across melanoma and NSCLC, baseline gut microbiome composition—measured by diversity and specific taxa or functional features—predicts response to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, while antibiotic exposure disrupts these beneficial profiles and diminishes ICI efficacy. Mechanistically, microbiota-driven modulation of PD-L2/RGMb signaling and immunostimulatory lipid features underpin these effects, and clinical data show that prior antibiotics are associated with reduced response rates and survival. Translational strategies that integrate microbiome profiling, targeted interventions, and judicious antibiotic stewardship are poised to personalize ICI therapy and improve outcomes. <cite id="37138075">The gut microbiome downregulates PD-L2/RGMb to promote anti-tumor immunity and responder microbiota can be transferred, but antibiotics negate these benefits</cite> <cite id="39929976">Hexa-acylated LPS in the microbiome predicts and augments anti-PD-1 responses, while LPS-binding antibiotics abolish efficacy in mice</cite> <cite id="32847937">Baseline antibiotics reduce diversity and beneficial taxa and correlate with worse survival in NSCLC</cite> <cite id="30885328">Antibiotic use is associated with shorter PFS and OS in NSCLC</cite> <cite id="40507352">A meta-analysis in melanoma shows pre-ICI antibiotics increase mortality risk by 26–55% depending on regimen and model</cite> <cite id="38588588">A randomized biomarker-stratified melanoma trial shows vancomycin disrupts microbiota and impairs immunity, underscoring the importance of antibiotic stewardship with ICI</cite>.

data.title: Gut microbiota-derived hexa-acylated lipopolysaccharides enhance cancer immunotherapy responses.
data.abstract: The gut microbiome modulates immunotherapy treatment responses, and this may explain why immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as anti-PD-1, are only effective in some patients. Previous studies correlated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-producing gut microbes with poorer prognosis; however, LPS from diverse bacterial species can range from immunostimulatory to inhibitory. Here, by functionally analysing faecal metagenomes from 112 patients with melanoma, we found that a subset of LPS-producing bacteria encoding immunostimulatory hexa-acylated LPS was enriched in microbiomes of clinical responders. In an implanted tumour mouse model of anti-PD-1 treatment, microbiota-derived hexa-acylated LPS was required for effective anti-tumour immune responses, and LPS-binding antibiotics and a small-molecule TLR4 antagonist abolished anti-PD-1 efficacy. Conversely, oral administration of hexa-acylated LPS to mice significantly augmented anti-PD-1-mediated anti-tumour immunity. Penta-acylated LPS did not improve anti-PD-1 efficacy in vivo and inhibited hexa-acylated LPS-induced immune activation in vitro. Microbiome hexa-acylated LPS therefore represents an accessible predictor and potential enhancer of immunotherapy responses.

data.title: The microbial metabolite desaminotyrosine enhances T-cell priming and cancer immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Inter-individual differences in response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) remain a major challenge in cancer treatment. The composition of the gut microbiome has been associated with differential ICI outcome, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear, and therapeutic modulation challenging.
METHODS
We established an in vivo model to treat C57Bl/6j mice with the type-I interferon (IFN-I)-modulating, bacterial-derived metabolite desaminotyrosine (DAT) to improve ICI therapy. Broad spectrum antibiotics were used to mimic gut microbial dysbiosis and associated ICI resistance. We utilized genetic mouse models to address the role of host IFN-I in DAT-modulated antitumour immunity. Changes in gut microbiota were assessed using 16S-rRNA sequencing analyses.
FINDINGS
We found that oral supplementation of mice with the microbial metabolite DAT delays tumour growth and promotes ICI immunotherapy with anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1. DAT-enhanced antitumour immunity was associated with more activated T cells and natural killer cells in the tumour microenvironment and was dependent on host IFN-I signalling. Consistent with this, DAT potently enhanced expansion of antigen-specific T cells following vaccination with an IFN-I-inducing adjuvant. DAT supplementation in mice compensated for the negative effects of broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced dysbiosis on anti-CTLA-4-mediated antitumour immunity. Oral administration of DAT altered the gut microbial composition in mice with increased abundance of bacterial taxa that are associated with beneficial response to ICI immunotherapy.
INTERPRETATION
We introduce the therapeutic use of an IFN-I-modulating bacterial-derived metabolite to overcome resistance to ICI. This approach is a promising strategy particularly for patients with a history of broad-spectrum antibiotic use and associated loss of gut microbial diversity.
FUNDING
Melanoma Research Alliance, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, German Cancer Aid, Wilhelm Sander Foundation, Novartis Foundation.

Analysis of 14 accrued patients demonstrated that treatment with SER-401 + nivolumab was safe, with an overall response rate of 25% in the SER-401 arm and 67% in the placebo arm (though the study was underpowered related to poor accrual during the COVID-19 pandemic). Translational analyses demonstrated that vancomycin preconditioning was associated with the disruption of the gut microbiota and impaired immunity, with incomplete recovery at ICB administration (particularly in patients with high baseline Ruminococcaceae). These results have important implications for future microbiome modulation trials. data.title: Diosgenin promotes antitumor immunity and PD-1 antibody efficacy against melanoma by regulating intestinal microbiota.
data.abstract: Diosgenin, a natural steroidal saponin, can exert antitumor effect by regulating immune function and improving intestinal microbiota. The response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy is associated with intestinal microbiota and effector T cells in tumor microenvironment. We hypothesize that the modulation of diosgenin on intestinal microbiota can facilitate antitumor immunity and the therapeutic efficacy of PD-1 antibody. In melanoma-bearing C57BL/6 mice, we observed that the anti-melanoma effect of diosgenin relied more on antitumor immunity than direct tumor inhibition activity evidenced by obvious CD4 + /CD8 + T-cell infiltration and IFN-γ expression in tumor tissues, and it could improve the compositions of intestinal microbiota. Antibiotics impaired the therapeutic efficacy and immunity responses of diosgenin through disturbing intestinal microbiota, indicating the importance of intestinal microbiota in diosgenin's in vivo antitumor activity. More importantly, the combined administration of PD-1 antibody with diosgenin aggravated the tumor necrosis and apoptosis by eliciting augmented T-cell responses. Taken together, diosgenin can be used as a microecological regulator to induce antitumor immunity and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint antibody, making it more suitable for the treatment of malignant tumors.

data.title: Gut microbiota and dietary intervention: affecting immunotherapy efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer.
data.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 80-85% of all lung cancers. In recent years, treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has gradually improved the survival rate of patients with NSCLC, especially those in the advanced stages. ICIs can block the tolerance pathways that are overexpressed by tumor cells and maintain the protective activity of immune system components against cancer cells. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that gut microbiota may modulate responses to ICIs treatment, possibly holding a key role in tumor immune surveillance and the efficacy of ICIs. Studies have also shown that diet can influence the abundance of gut microbiota in humans, therefore, dietary interventions and the adjustment of the gut microbiota is a novel and promising treatment strategy for adjunctive cancer therapy. This review comprehensively summarizes the effects of gut microbiota, antibiotics (ATBs), and dietary intervention on the efficacy of immunotherapy in NSCLC, with the aim of informing the development of novel strategies in NSCLC immunotherapy.

data.title: The Gut Microbiome Associates with Immune Checkpoint Inhibition Outcomes in Patients with Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
data.abstract: The gut microbiome (GM) plays an important role in shaping systemic immune responses and influences immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy. Antibiotics worsen clinical outcomes in patients receiving ICI. However, whether GM profiling and baseline antibiotic can be a biomarker of ICI efficacy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains unknown. We prospectively collected baseline (pre-ICI) fecal samples and clinical data of 70 Japanese patients suffering from advanced NSCLC and treated them with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies as a first-line or treatment-refractory therapy. We performed 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing of gene amplicons of fecal samples, and bacteria diversity and differential abundance analysis was performed. The clinical endpoints were objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and immune-related adverse events (irAE). ORR was 34%, and median PFS and OS were 5.2 and 16.2 months, respectively. Patients who received pre-ICI antibiotic had lower alpha diversity at baseline and underrepresentation of Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter When analyzing antibiotic-free patients, alpha diversity correlated with OS. In addition, Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 and Agathobacter were enriched in patients with favorable ORR and PFS >6 months. Ruminococcaceae UCG 13 was enriched in patients with OS >12 months. GM differences were observed between patients who experienced low- versus high-grade irAE. We demonstrated the negative influence of antibiotic on the GM composition and identified the bacteria repertoire in patients experiencing favorable responses to ICI. See articles by Tomita et al., p. 1236, and Peng et al., p. 1251 .

data.title: Distinct Functional Metagenomic Markers Predict the Responsiveness to Anti-PD-1 Therapy in Chinese Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Programmed death 1 (PD-1) and the ligand of PD-1 (PD-L1) are central targets for immune-checkpoint therapy (ICT) blocking immune evasion-related pathways elicited by tumor cells. A number of PD-1 inhibitors have been developed, but the efficacy of these inhibitors varies considerably and is typically below 50%. The efficacy of ICT has been shown to be dependent on the gut microbiota, and experiments using mouse models have even demonstrated that modulation of the gut microbiota may improve efficacy of ICT.
METHODS
We followed a Han Chinese cohort of 85 advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, who received anti-PD-1 antibodies. Tumor biopsies were collected before treatment initiation for whole exon sequencing and variant detection. Fecal samples collected biweekly during the period of anti-PD-1 antibody administration were used for metagenomic sequencing. We established gut microbiome abundance profiles for identification of significant associations between specific microbial taxa, potential functionality, and treatment responses. A prediction model based on random forest was trained using selected markers discriminating between the different response groups.
RESULTS
NSCLC patients treated with antibiotics exhibited the shortest survival time. Low level of tumor-mutation burden and high expression level of HLA-E significantly reduced progression-free survival. We identified metagenomic species and functional pathways that differed in abundance in relation to responses to ICT. Data on differential enrichment of taxa and predicted microbial functions in NSCLC patients responding or non-responding to ICT allowed the establishment of random forest algorithm-adopted models robustly predicting the probability of whether or not a given patient would benefit from ICT.
CONCLUSIONS
Overall, our results identified links between gut microbial composition and immunotherapy efficacy in Chinese NSCLC patients indicating the potential for such analyses to predict outcome prior to ICT.

data.title: Antibiotics are associated with attenuated efficacy of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies in Chinese patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Gut microbiome plays a dominant role in modulating therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death receptor/ligand-1 (PD-1/PD-L1) pathway, suggesting that co-administration of antibiotics (Abx), which might result in dysbacteriosis, can attenuate the clinical outcomes of ICIs. The current study aimed to investigate the predictive role of Abx on ICIs treatment in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The impact of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), another medication that can induce dysbacteriosis, was also investigated.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of eligible patients who received anti-PD-1-based therapies in our hospital. Tumor responses, patients' survival, the incidence of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) and other baseline variables were examined. The application of Abx or PPIs treatment were also collected. Clinical outcomes and clinicopathologic features were compared according to the status of Abx or PPIs co-administration.
RESULTS
A total of 109 patients were included. Of them, 20 (18.3%) patients were categorized in Abx-treated group. No major difference in baseline characteristics was observed between Abx-treated and -untreated groups. Concomitant Abx treatment was significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (p < 0.0001) and overall survival (OS) (p = 0.0021). And primary disease progression tended to increase in Abx-treated group (p = 0.092). Yet, the occurrence and grades of irAEs were comparable between two groups. In multivariable analysis, Abx treatment was markedly associated with worse PFS (HR=0.32, 95%CI 0.18-0.59, p < 0.0001) and OS (HR=0.35, 95%CI 0.16-0.77, p = 0.009). Regarding the use of PPIs, no significant difference was observed in clinical outcomes between the patients with or without concomitant PPIs treatment.
CONCLUSIONS
Abx treatment was significantly associated with attenuated clinical outcomes derived from anti-PD-1-based ICIs in a Chinese cohort of patients with advanced NSCLC.

data.title: The Use of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Oncology and the Occurrence of AKI: Where Do We Stand?
data.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are a novel class of immunotherapy drugs that have improved the treatment of a broad spectrum of cancers as metastatic melanoma, non-small lung cancer or renal cell carcinoma. These humanized monoclonal antibodies target inhibitory receptors (e.g. CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and ligands (PD-L1) expressed on T lymphocytes, antigen presenting cells and tumor cells and elicit an anti-tumor response by stimulating immune system. Nevertheless, the improved overall survival is complicated by the manifestation of Immune-related Adverse Effects (irAEs). During treatment with ICIs, the most common adverse kidney effect is represented by the development of acute kidney injury (AKI) with the acute tubulointerstitial nephritis as recurrent histological feature. The mechanisms involved in ICIs-induced AKI include the re-activation of effector T cells previously stimulated by nephrotoxic drugs (i.e. by antibiotics), the loss of tolerance versus self-renal antigens, the increased PD-L1 expression by tubular cells or the establishment of a pro-inflammatory milieu with the release of self-reactive antibodies. For renal transplant recipient treated with ICIs, the increased incidence of rejection is a serious concern. Therefore, the combination of ICIs with mTOR inhibitors represents an emerging strategy. Finally, it is relevant to anticipate which patients under ICIs would experience severe irAEs and from a kidney perspective, to predict patients with higher risk of AKI. Here, we provide a detailed overview of ICIs-related nephrotoxicity and the recently described multicenter studies. Several factors have been reported as biomarkers of ICIs-irAEs, in this review we speculate on potential biomarkers for ICIs-associated AKI.
