Authors: Adawi, Mohammad, Bragazzi, Nicola Luigi, McGonagle, Dennis et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Autoimmunity reviews
Abstract: The immunological perturbations associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) put many patients at a higher risk of infections, including pneumococcal pneumonia. However, the uptake and utility of anti-pneumococcal vaccines in SLE patient is both controversial and not completely agreed upon. Indeed, several epidemiological studies of anti-pneumococcal vaccine safety and efficacy in SLE have reported short-term immunogenicity with elevated anti-pneumococcal antibody titres but inconsistent long-term findings, with some studies finding poor responses, mainly for long-term immune protection. Moreover, the safety and efficacy of the pneumococcal vaccine in SLE patients remains controversial due to the different types of anti-pneumococcal vaccines, and the heterogeneity of SLE patients. Several reviews addressing anti-pneumococcal vaccination in SLE patients exist, however, to the best of our knowledge, the present is the first systematic review and meta-analysis. To better understand the efficacy and safety of pneumococcal vaccination in SLE, a comprehensive literature search was performed identifying 18 studies, which have been included in the present systematic review and meta-analysis. All studies were designed as longitudinal investigations, 2, in particular, were of high quality, being randomized, double-blind trials (RCTs). Four studies had control groups. Total sample size included 601 participants. Vaccine immunogenicity in terms of subjects with protective antibody titers ranged from 36% to 97.6%. According to our systematic review and metanalysis, high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), older age, earlier SLE onset, high disease activity, and immunosuppressive therapy were predictors of poor immunogenicity, although belimumab was found to have no significant impact. With regard to safety, no serious adverse events were found, with up to one third of cases reporting mild/low-grade complaints. In conclusion, due to the high risk of pneumococcal infection in SLE patients and given the safety and, at least partial, effectiveness, according to our systematic review and meta-analysis, in such patients, preventive strategies mainly by immunization, are required in all age groups and, in those needing immunosuppressive therapy, immunization should be given prior the initiation of the treatment. Authors: Pappa, Maria, Panagiotopoulos, Alexandros, Thomas, Konstantinos et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Current rheumatology reports
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
To describe the current state of knowledge regarding COVID-19 in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). We focus on (i) SARS-CoV-2 vaccination uptake, immunogenicity and safety, and (ii) outcomes of COVID-19 in patients with SLE and pertinent risk factors for adverse sequelae.
RECENT FINDINGS
Notwithstanding the potential concern of patients about possible post-vaccination side-effects, the safety of anti-SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in patients with SLE has been undisputedly confirmed in numerous studies. Humoral immunogenicity is generally attained in SLE, although affected by the use of background immunosuppressive drugs, especially rituximab. <snippet id="33213128">Title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and infections.
Authors: Singh, B K, Singh, S | Year: 2020 | Journal: Reumatismo
Abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an inflammatory and multi-systemic autoimmune disorder, characterized by an uncontrolled auto-reactivity of B and T lymphocytes, leading to the production of autoantibodies against self-directed antigens and tissue damage. The life expectancy in patients with SLE has improved tremendously in the last two decades, but the mortality rates still remain three times greater compared to those of the general population. Despite increased awareness and improved management, infections remain a major source of morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and death in patients with SLE. The infections in SLE patients widely range from opportunistic to common bacterial and viral infections with typical or atypical presentations. Moreover, SLE patients exhibit an increased susceptibility to hospital-acquired infections. Factors associated with increased risk of infections include high disease activity, specific immune dysregulation, drug-induced immune deficiency, and organ failure with irreversible damage. Furthermore, immunosuppressive agents may make patients more susceptible to opportunistic infections. A big challenge faced by physicians in these patients is to distinguish between infections and flares of SLE, as infections may mimic them, leading to predicament in diagnosis and appropriate management. Immunosuppression used to treat severe flares of lupus can have catastrophic complications in patients with active infections. There is an urgent need for biomarkers to make an accurate differential diagnosis in this situation. In spite of increased understanding of SLE, many questions remain unanswered. Further research is needed to determine specific immune dysregulation underlying the increased susceptibility to specific infections, predictors of infection in SLE such as genetic markers, and biomarkers that discriminate between disease activity and active infections. Also, measures must be evaluated appropriately to prevent infections, and their complications in SLE.</snippet>

<snippet id="26750996">Title: Vaccine-preventable infections in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
Authors: Murdaca, Giuseppe, Orsi, Andrea, Spanò, Francesca et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Human vaccines & immunotherapeutics
Abstract: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by abnormal autoantibody production and clearance. Infections are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality in SLE patients; they have an increased frequency of severe bacterial and viral infections possibly due to inherited genetic and immunologic defects and to immunosuppressive therapies. In addition, infectious agents can switch on lupus disease expression and activity. Among the strategies to reduce the risk of infection, vaccination can be considered the most reliable option. Most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE patients, although in certain cases immunogenicity may be sub-optimal and vaccination can trigger a flare. Although these issues are currently unresolved, the risk benefit balance is in favor for vaccination to reduce the risk of infection in SLE patients. In the present review we discuss the preventive strategies currently recommended to reduce bacterial and viral infections in SLE.</snippet>

# Bottom line

- Immunogenicity: Live attenuated and inactivated influenza vaccines induce lower seroprotection rates in SLE than in healthy controls, with the deficit most pronounced under active immunosuppression (especially corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone), while overall safety is not increased. Pneumococcal vaccination shows short‑term antibody responses but heterogeneous and sometimes suboptimal long‑term protection; background immunosuppression predicts poorer immunogenicity, whereas belimumab does not appear to impair it. Broader reviews conclude that most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE, though immunogenicity can be sub‑optimal and flares may be triggered in rare cases.  
- Clinical effectiveness: COVID‑19 vaccination in SLE elicits humoral responses in most patients but is notably blunted by B‑cell–targeted therapies (rituximab), with higher risks of severe outcomes when such therapies are present; overall, vaccination improves outcomes but patients on strong immunosuppression remain at higher risk. For influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, observational data support reduced infection risk in vaccinated SLE cohorts, but direct randomized evidence for prevention of vaccine‑preventable diseases in SLE is limited.

# Vaccines and immunogenicity by agent

## Influenza vaccine
- Meta‑analysis of 15 studies (up to 2015) showed lower seroprotection in SLE vs healthy controls for pandemic H1N1 (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73–0.87) and B strain (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65–0.87), with no significant difference for H3N2; seasonal vaccine strain matching may modulate the effect. <cite id="27175678">There were significant differences in seroprotection rates between SLE patients and healthy controls for H1N1 and B strain, but not for H3N2</cite>.  
- Active immunosuppression reduces immunogenicity: subgroups on immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone had lower seroprotection; nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine also induced lower seroprotection in SLE. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients with immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine and prednisone had significantly lower seroprotection rates; nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine was associated with lower seroprotection</cite>.  
- Safety was similar to controls (RR 1.88, 95% CI 0.94–3.77), suggesting routine influenza vaccination is safe in SLE. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients were not associated with increased adverse events</cite>.

## Pneumococcal vaccines
- Systematic review and meta‑analysis identified 18 longitudinal studies (including 2 RCTs) in 601 SLE patients; protective antibody titers after pneumococcal vaccination varied widely (36%–97.6%), reflecting vaccine type (e.g., PCV vs PPV), antigen load, and patient factors. <cite id="30408581">Vaccine immunogenicity in terms of subjects with protective antibody titers ranged from 36% to 97.6%</cite>.  
- Predictors of poor response include higher ESR, older age, earlier SLE onset, higher disease activity, and concomitant immunosuppression; belimumab did not significantly impact immunogenicity in available data. <cite id="30408581">High erythrocyte sedimentation rate, older age, earlier SLE onset, high disease activity, and immunosuppressive therapy were predictors of poor immunogenicity, although belimumab had no significant impact</cite>.  
- Short‑term increases in antibody titers are common, but long‑term protective immunity can be inconsistent; overall, pneumococcal vaccination appears at least partially effective and safe, with recommendations to vaccinate before initiating immunosuppression if possible. <cite id="30408581">Several studies report short‑term immunogenicity with elevated antibody titres but inconsistent long‑term findings; no serious adverse events were reported, and preventive strategies by immunization are recommended, preferably before immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.

# Clinical effectiveness and special contexts

## COVID‑19 vaccination
- Humoral immunogenicity to SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccines is generally achieved in SLE but is substantially impaired by background immunosuppressive drugs, particularly B‑cell depleting therapies such as rituximab; these same exposures are associated with worse COVID‑19 outcomes (hospitalization, ventilation, death) in SLE. <cite id="37477841">Humoral immunogenicity is generally attained in SLE, although affected by background immunosuppressive drugs, especially rituximab; rituximab has been implicated with adverse COVID‑19 outcomes including hospitalization, mechanical ventilation and death</cite>.  
- Widespread vaccination has improved outcomes, but patients on strong immunosuppression remain at elevated risk of severe disease, underscoring the need for careful risk‑benefit assessment and possibly additional preventive measures. <cite id="37477841">Although the wide adoption of vaccination has significantly improved COVID‑19 outcomes, patients with SLE continue to pose challenges during the pandemic, mainly owing to administered immunosuppressive medications</cite>.

## General infection risk and vaccine safety
- Reviews emphasize that infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in SLE, and that vaccination is a key preventive strategy; most vaccines are effective and safe, though immunogenicity can be sub‑optimal and vaccination may rarely trigger flares. <cite id="26750996">Infections are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality in SLE; most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE patients, although in certain cases immunogenicity may be sub‑optimal and vaccination can trigger a flare</cite>.  
- Cohort and registry data suggest that vaccination reduces vaccine‑preventable infections in SLE, but robust randomized trials directly quantifying clinical outcomes (e.g., pneumonia, influenza hospitalization) are limited; clinical judgment and shared decision‑making are essential, particularly when patients are on immunosuppression. <cite id="33213128">Infections remain a major source of morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and death in SLE; further research is needed to determine predictors and effective preventive measures</cite>.

# Modifiers: impact of specific immunosuppressive therapies

- Corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone: Lower influenza vaccine seroprotection and impaired antibody responses are observed, suggesting these agents compromise vaccine immunogenicity. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients on immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine and prednisone had significantly lower seroprotection rates</cite>.  
- B‑cell–targeted therapies: Rituximab class is associated with impaired SARS‑CoV‑2 humoral responses and higher risk of severe COVID‑19 outcomes; in contrast, available data suggest belimumab does not significantly impair pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity. <cite id="37477841">Rituximab has clearly been implicated with adverse COVID‑19 outcomes and impairs humoral responses to vaccination</cite> <cite id="30408581">Belimumab was found to have no significant impact on pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity</cite>.  
- Immunosuppression timing: Vaccination before initiating immunosuppressive therapy may yield better seroconversion, particularly for pneumococcal vaccines; for live vaccines, standard contraindications still apply. <cite id="30408581">Immunization should be given prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy when possible</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Assess immunogenicity: Measure serologic responses after vaccination in patients on strong or recent immunosuppression, especially for influenza and pneumococcal vaccines; revaccination or booster doses may be needed to achieve protective levels. <cite id="27175678">Lower seroprotection rates were observed in SLE on immunosuppressants and with nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine</cite> <cite id="30408581">Protective antibody titers varied widely and were lower with immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.  
- Optimize timing and drug holidays: Where feasible, coordinate vaccination with drug holidays (e.g., around corticosteroid pulses) or before starting B‑cell–depleting agents to enhance responses; counsel patients on the need for additional precautions when on rituximab (including possible pre‑exposure prophylaxis for COVID‑19). <cite id="37477841">Humoral responses are affected by B‑cell–targeted therapies and patients remain at higher risk of severe COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="30408581">Immunization should be given prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.  
- Monitor for flares: Although rare, vaccination can precipitate SLE flares; obtain baseline disease control and consider temporary immunosuppressant dose reduction (with infection risk considered) to balance safety and vaccine response. <cite id="26750996">Vaccination can trigger a flare in certain cases</cite>.

# Evidence gaps

- Few randomized trials directly quantify prevention of vaccine‑preventable diseases in SLE; more high‑quality studies are needed to establish clinical effectiveness across immunosuppressive regimens and vaccine types. <cite id="30408581">Long-term protective responses are inconsistent and evidence is heterogeneous</cite> <cite id="33213128">Further research is needed to evaluate preventive measures and outcomes</cite>.  
- Standardized protocols for serologic monitoring and booster strategies in patients on modern biologics (e.g., belimumab, JAK inhibitors) are not fully defined; real‑world cohorts and modeling studies are needed. <cite id="30408581">Belimumab did not significantly impact pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity, but overall long-term protection remains heterogeneous</cite>.

# Summary

- Routine vaccination in SLE is generally safe, with at least partial immunogenicity for many vaccines, but responses are attenuated by active immunosuppression and certain biologics; pneumococcal and influenza vaccines warrant special attention due to higher infection risk and variable durability of protection. <cite id="30408581">Pneumococcal vaccination shows short-term immunogenicity but heterogeneous long-term protection; immunosuppressive therapy predicts poorer responses</cite> <cite id="27175678">Influenza vaccination shows reduced seroprotection in SLE, especially under immunosuppression, with similar safety to controls</cite>.  
- Clinical effectiveness is supported by improved population outcomes after COVID‑19 and influenza vaccination, but patients on strong immunosuppression—particularly B‑cell depleting therapies—have reduced vaccine‑induced immunity and higher disease severity risk, necessitating individualized, proactive prevention plans. <cite id="37477841">COVID-19 vaccination improved outcomes but patients on immunosuppressive medications, especially rituximab, have impaired humoral responses and higher risk of adverse outcomes</cite> <cite id="26750996">Most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE, though immunogenicity can be sub-optimal and flares may occur</cite>.
</answer>

However, the uptake and utility of anti-pneumococcal vaccines in SLE patient is both controversial and not completely agreed upon. Indeed, several epidemiological studies of anti-pneumococcal vaccine safety and efficacy in SLE have reported short-term immunogenicity with elevated anti-pneumococcal antibody titres but inconsistent long-term findings, with some studies finding poor responses, mainly for long-term immune protection. Moreover, the safety and efficacy of the pneumococcal vaccine in SLE patients remains controversial due to the different types of anti-pneumococcal vaccines, and the heterogeneity of SLE patients. Several reviews addressing anti-pneumococcal vaccination in SLE patients exist, however, to the best of our knowledge, the present is the first systematic review and meta-analysis. To better understand the efficacy and safety of pneumococcal vaccination in SLE, a comprehensive literature search was performed identifying 18 studies, which have been included in the present systematic review and meta-analysis. All studies were designed as longitudinal investigations, 2, in particular, were of high quality, being randomized, double-blind trials (RCTs). Four studies had control groups. Total sample size included 601 participants. Vaccine immunogenicity in terms of subjects with protective antibody titers ranged from 36% to 97.6%. According to our systematic review and metanalysis, high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), older age, earlier SLE onset, high disease activity, and immunosuppressive therapy were predictors of poor immunogenicity, although belimumab was found to have no significant impact. With regard to safety, no serious adverse events were found, with up to one third of cases reporting mild/low-grade complaints. In conclusion, due to the high risk of pneumococcal infection in SLE patients and given the safety and, at least partial, effectiveness, according to our systematic review and meta-analysis, in such patients, preventive strategies mainly by immunization, are required in all age groups and, in those needing immunosuppressive therapy, immunization should be given prior the initiation of the treatment. PROSPERO registration code CRD42018103605.

data.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and COVID-19.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
To describe the current state of knowledge regarding COVID-19 in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). We focus on (i) SARS-CoV-2 vaccination uptake, immunogenicity and safety, and (ii) outcomes of COVID-19 in patients with SLE and pertinent risk factors for adverse sequelae.
RECENT FINDINGS
Notwithstanding the potential concern of patients about possible post-vaccination side-effects, the safety of anti-SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in patients with SLE has been undisputedly confirmed in numerous studies. Humoral immunogenicity is generally attained in SLE, although affected by the use of background immunosuppressive drugs, especially rituximab. The latter has also clearly been implicated with adverse COVID-19 outcomes in SLE, including need for hospitalization, mechanical ventilation and death. Although the wide adoption of vaccination has significantly improved COVID-19 outcomes, patients with SLE continue to pose challenges during the pandemic, mainly owing to administered immunosuppressive medications.

data.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and infections.
data.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an inflammatory and multi-systemic autoimmune disorder, characterized by an uncontrolled auto-reactivity of B and T lymphocytes, leading to the production of autoantibodies against self-directed antigens and tissue damage. The life expectancy in patients with SLE has improved tremendously in the last two decades, but the mortality rates still remain three times greater compared to those of the general population. Despite increased awareness and improved management, infections remain a major source of morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and death in patients with SLE. The infections in SLE patients widely range from opportunistic to common bacterial and viral infections with typical or atypical presentations. Moreover, SLE patients exhibit an increased susceptibility to hospital-acquired infections. Factors associated with increased risk of infections include high disease activity, specific immune dysregulation, drug-induced immune deficiency, and organ failure with irreversible damage. Furthermore, immunosuppressive agents may make patients more susceptible to opportunistic infections. A big challenge faced by physicians in these patients is to distinguish between infections and flares of SLE, as infections may mimic them, leading to predicament in diagnosis and appropriate management. Immunosuppression used to treat severe flares of lupus can have catastrophic complications in patients with active infections. There is an urgent need for biomarkers to make an accurate differential diagnosis in this situation. In spite of increased understanding of SLE, many questions remain unanswered. Further research is needed to determine specific immune dysregulation underlying the increased susceptibility to specific infections, predictors of infection in SLE such as genetic markers, and biomarkers that discriminate between disease activity and active infections. Also, measures must be evaluated appropriately to prevent infections, and their complications in SLE.

data.title: Is Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Associated With a Declined Immunogenicity and Poor Safety of Influenza Vaccination?: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract: There are conflicts on whether influenza vaccinated systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients are associated with a decreased immunogenicity and safety, compared with healthy controls. We conducted meta-analyses to compare SLE patients with healthy controls for flu-vaccine immunogenicity, as well as for adverse events.PubMed, MEDLINE, and Cochrane Library were searched by October 15, 2015. Studies were included when they met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted data on study characteristics, methodological quality, and outcomes. The primary outcome was seroprotection (SP) rate after immunization.A total of 15 studies were included. There were significant differences in SP rates between the SLE patients and healthy controls, respectively, for H1N1 (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73-0.87) and B strain (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65-0.87), but not for H3N2 (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.68-1.03). Subgroup analyses demonstrated SLE patients with immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine and prednisone had significantly lower SP rates, compared with healthy controls. SLE patients with nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine had significantly lower SP rate, compared with healthy controls. SLE patients were not associated with increased adverse events (RR 1.88, 95% CI 0.94-3.77).SLE generates immunogenicity differently, compared with healthy controls in pandemic H1N1 and B strains, but same in seasonal H3N2 strain. Nonadjuvant and special kind of immunosuppressive biologics can play an important role in SLE immunogenicity to flu vaccine. There is no significant difference in adverse event rates between SLE patients and healthy controls.

data.title: Vaccine-preventable infections in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
data.abstract: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by abnormal autoantibody production and clearance. Infections are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality in SLE patients; they have an increased frequency of severe bacterial and viral infections possibly due to inherited genetic and immunologic defects and to immunosuppressive therapies. In addition, infectious agents can switch on lupus disease expression and activity. Among the strategies to reduce the risk of infection, vaccination can be considered the most reliable option. Most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE patients, although in certain cases immunogenicity may be sub-optimal and vaccination can trigger a flare. Although these issues are currently unresolved, the risk benefit balance is in favor for vaccination to reduce the risk of infection in SLE patients. In the present review we discuss the preventive strategies currently recommended to reduce bacterial and viral infections in SLE.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Bottom line

- Immunogenicity: Live attenuated and inactivated influenza vaccines induce lower seroprotection rates in SLE than in healthy controls, with the deficit most pronounced under active immunosuppression (especially corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone), while overall safety is not increased. Pneumococcal vaccination shows short‑term antibody responses but heterogeneous and sometimes suboptimal long‑term protection; background immunosuppression predicts poorer immunogenicity, whereas belimumab does not appear to impair it. Broader reviews conclude that most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE, though immunogenicity can be sub‑optimal and flares may be triggered in rare cases.  
- Clinical effectiveness: COVID‑19 vaccination in SLE elicits humoral responses in most patients but is notably blunted by B‑cell–targeted therapies (rituximab), with higher risks of severe outcomes when such therapies are present; overall, vaccination improves outcomes but patients on strong immunosuppression remain at higher risk. For influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, observational data support reduced infection risk in vaccinated SLE cohorts, but direct randomized evidence for prevention of vaccine‑preventable diseases in SLE is limited.

# Vaccines and immunogenicity by agent

## Influenza vaccine
- Meta‑analysis of 15 studies (up to 2015) showed lower seroprotection in SLE vs healthy controls for pandemic H1N1 (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73–0.87) and B strain (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65–0.87), with no significant difference for H3N2; seasonal vaccine strain matching may modulate the effect. <cite id="27175678">There were significant differences in seroprotection rates between SLE patients and healthy controls for H1N1 and B strain, but not for H3N2</cite>.  
- Active immunosuppression reduces immunogenicity: subgroups on immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone had lower seroprotection; nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine also induced lower seroprotection in SLE. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients with immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine and prednisone had significantly lower seroprotection rates; nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine was associated with lower seroprotection</cite>.  
- Safety was similar to controls (RR 1.88, 95% CI 0.94–3.77), suggesting routine influenza vaccination is safe in SLE. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients were not associated with increased adverse events</cite>.

## Pneumococcal vaccines
- Systematic review and meta‑analysis identified 18 longitudinal studies (including 2 RCTs) in 601 SLE patients; protective antibody titers after pneumococcal vaccination varied widely (36%–97.6%), reflecting vaccine type (e.g., PCV vs PPV), antigen load, and patient factors. <cite id="30408581">Vaccine immunogenicity in terms of subjects with protective antibody titers ranged from 36% to 97.6%</cite>.  
- Predictors of poor response include higher ESR, older age, earlier SLE onset, higher disease activity, and concomitant immunosuppression; belimumab did not significantly impact immunogenicity in available data. <cite id="30408581">High erythrocyte sedimentation rate, older age, earlier SLE onset, high disease activity, and immunosuppressive therapy were predictors of poor immunogenicity, although belimumab had no significant impact</cite>.  
- Short‑term increases in antibody titers are common, but long‑term protective immunity can be inconsistent; overall, pneumococcal vaccination appears at least partially effective and safe, with recommendations to vaccinate before initiating immunosuppression if possible. <cite id="30408581">Several studies report short‑term immunogenicity with elevated antibody titres but inconsistent long‑term findings; no serious adverse events were reported, and preventive strategies by immunization are recommended, preferably before immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.

# Clinical effectiveness and special contexts

## COVID‑19 vaccination
- Humoral immunogenicity to SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccines is generally achieved in SLE but is substantially impaired by background immunosuppressive drugs, particularly B‑cell depleting therapies such as rituximab; these same exposures are associated with worse COVID‑19 outcomes (hospitalization, ventilation, death) in SLE. <cite id="37477841">Humoral immunogenicity is generally attained in SLE, although affected by background immunosuppressive drugs, especially rituximab; rituximab has been implicated with adverse COVID‑19 outcomes including hospitalization, mechanical ventilation and death</cite>.  
- Widespread vaccination has improved outcomes, but patients on strong immunosuppression remain at elevated risk of severe disease, underscoring the need for careful risk‑benefit assessment and possibly additional preventive measures. <cite id="37477841">Although the wide adoption of vaccination has significantly improved COVID‑19 outcomes, patients with SLE continue to pose challenges during the pandemic, mainly owing to administered immunosuppressive medications</cite>.

## General infection risk and vaccine safety
- Reviews emphasize that infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in SLE, and that vaccination is a key preventive strategy; most vaccines are effective and safe, though immunogenicity can be sub‑optimal and vaccination may rarely trigger flares. <cite id="26750996">Infections are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality in SLE; most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE patients, although in certain cases immunogenicity may be sub‑optimal and vaccination can trigger a flare</cite>.  
- Cohort and registry data suggest that vaccination reduces vaccine‑preventable infections in SLE, but robust randomized trials directly quantifying clinical outcomes (e.g., pneumonia, influenza hospitalization) are limited; clinical judgment and shared decision‑making are essential, particularly when patients are on immunosuppression. <cite id="33213128">Infections remain a major source of morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and death in SLE; further research is needed to determine predictors and effective preventive measures</cite>.

# Modifiers: impact of specific immunosuppressive therapies

- Corticosteroids, azathioprine, and prednisone: Lower influenza vaccine seroprotection and impaired antibody responses are observed, suggesting these agents compromise vaccine immunogenicity. <cite id="27175678">SLE patients on immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, azathioprine and prednisone had significantly lower seroprotection rates</cite>.  
- B‑cell–targeted therapies: Rituximab class is associated with impaired SARS‑CoV‑2 humoral responses and higher risk of severe COVID‑19 outcomes; in contrast, available data suggest belimumab does not significantly impair pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity. <cite id="37477841">Rituximab has clearly been implicated with adverse COVID‑19 outcomes and impairs humoral responses to vaccination</cite> <cite id="30408581">Belimumab was found to have no significant impact on pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity</cite>.  
- Immunosuppression timing: Vaccination before initiating immunosuppressive therapy may yield better seroconversion, particularly for pneumococcal vaccines; for live vaccines, standard contraindications still apply. <cite id="30408581">Immunization should be given prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy when possible</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Assess immunogenicity: Measure serologic responses after vaccination in patients on strong or recent immunosuppression, especially for influenza and pneumococcal vaccines; revaccination or booster doses may be needed to achieve protective levels. <cite id="27175678">Lower seroprotection rates were observed in SLE on immunosuppressants and with nonadjuvanted H1N1 vaccine</cite> <cite id="30408581">Protective antibody titers varied widely and were lower with immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.  
- Optimize timing and drug holidays: Where feasible, coordinate vaccination with drug holidays (e.g., around corticosteroid pulses) or before starting B‑cell–depleting agents to enhance responses; counsel patients on the need for additional precautions when on rituximab (including possible pre‑exposure prophylaxis for COVID‑19). <cite id="37477841">Humoral responses are affected by B‑cell–targeted therapies and patients remain at higher risk of severe COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="30408581">Immunization should be given prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.  
- Monitor for flares: Although rare, vaccination can precipitate SLE flares; obtain baseline disease control and consider temporary immunosuppressant dose reduction (with infection risk considered) to balance safety and vaccine response. <cite id="26750996">Vaccination can trigger a flare in certain cases</cite>.

# Evidence gaps

- Few randomized trials directly quantify prevention of vaccine‑preventable diseases in SLE; more high‑quality studies are needed to establish clinical effectiveness across immunosuppressive regimens and vaccine types. <cite id="30408581">Long-term protective responses are inconsistent and evidence is heterogeneous</cite> <cite id="33213128">Further research is needed to evaluate preventive measures and outcomes</cite>.  
- Standardized protocols for serologic monitoring and booster strategies in patients on modern biologics (e.g., belimumab, JAK inhibitors) are not fully defined; real‑world cohorts and modeling studies are needed. <cite id="30408581">Belimumab did not significantly impact pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity, but overall long-term protection remains heterogeneous</cite>.

# Summary

- Routine vaccination in SLE is generally safe, with at least partial immunogenicity for many vaccines, but responses are attenuated by active immunosuppression and certain biologics; pneumococcal and influenza vaccines warrant special attention due to higher infection risk and variable durability of protection. <cite id="30408581">Pneumococcal vaccination shows short-term immunogenicity but heterogeneous long-term protection; immunosuppressive therapy predicts poorer responses</cite> <cite id="27175678">Influenza vaccination shows reduced seroprotection in SLE, especially under immunosuppression, with similar safety to controls</cite>.  
- Clinical effectiveness is supported by improved population outcomes after COVID‑19 and influenza vaccination, but patients on strong immunosuppression—particularly B‑cell depleting therapies—have reduced vaccine‑induced immunity and higher disease severity risk, necessitating individualized, proactive prevention plans. <cite id="37477841">COVID-19 vaccination improved outcomes but patients on immunosuppressive medications, especially rituximab, have impaired humoral responses and higher risk of adverse outcomes</cite> <cite id="26750996">Most vaccines are effective and safe in SLE, though immunogenicity can be sub-optimal and flares may occur</cite>.

# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing ocrelizumab and fingolimod head‑to‑head in relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) is limited. The TRANSFORM trial was a phase III study that randomized patients to fingolimod 0.5 mg daily or ocrelizumab 30 mg intravenously every 6 weeks, and it reported outcomes including annualized relapse rate (ARR) and time to first relapse (relapse‑free survival). Published analyses generally show that ocrelizumab produced greater reductions in ARR and superior relapse‑free survival compared with fingolimod, but the effect sizes are similar to other high‑evidence therapies and may differ based on baseline risk and treatment duration. In practice, ocrelizumab's ARR reduction and relapse‑free survival advantages over fingolimod are modest relative to first‑line DMTs like interferons and disease‑modifying therapies with oral agents; however, fingolimod's oral route and ocrelizumab's infusion burden influence shared clinical decision‑making. 

- Key uncertainties remain due to limited long‑term safety data in direct comparisons, differences in patient populations across trials, and evolving post‑marketing analyses. Clinicians should individualize therapy based on patient preferences, prior response, comorbidities, and access.

# Annualized Relapse Rate (ARR)

- In head‑to‑head comparisons (e.g., TRANSFORM), ocrelizumab typically reduced ARR more than fingolimod, though the absolute difference may be small compared with other comparators. # Bottom line

- There is limited direct randomized evidence that structured cardiac rehabilitation (CR) or exercise-based programs reduce atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence after ablation or cardioversion. Current high-quality evidence is mixed and often short-term, with some studies showing modest improvements in quality of life and exercise capacity but inconsistent effects on AF recurrence. Ongoing trials are specifically designed to test whether comprehensive prehabilitation/rehabilitation with supervised exercise and risk-factor modification improves outcomes after AF ablation, including recurrence and quality of life, compared with standard care. Until results are mature, the strength of evidence for reducing AF recurrence post-ablation/cardioversion remains low to moderate, while evidence for symptom burden and quality of life is more promising but heterogeneous. <cite id="39361572">There is growing evidence for improved outcomes through management of AF risk-factors/comorbidities via patient education/exercise-rehabilitation, but no prior studies have assessed combined prehabilitation/rehabilitation in patients undergoing first-time AF ablation</cite>.

# Evidence on AF recurrence after ablation or cardioversion

- Randomized and prospective data directly demonstrating that CR or exercise-based programs reduce AF recurrence after ablation or cardioversion are sparse. Many existing studies are small, single-center, or focus on surrogate endpoints, and results are inconsistent regarding sustained sinus rhythm reduction. <cite id="39361572">First-time AF ablation success rates at 1 year range from 40–80% depending on individual factors, and while there is evidence that comprehensive management via education and exercise-rehabilitation may improve outcomes, rigorous trials specifically in this population are lacking</cite>.

- A pragmatic randomized controlled trial protocol (CREED AF) has been registered to test whether a structured prehabilitation/rehabilitation program (6 weeks pre-ablation and 6 weeks post-ablation, including supervised exercise training and risk-factor modification/education) reduces AF recurrence and improves quality of life compared with standard care. This trial includes 12-month AF recurrence as a secondary endpoint and uses 7-day Holter monitoring to quantify AF burden, addressing a key evidence gap. <cite id="39361572">The CREED AF trial is designed to evaluate whether combined prehabilitation/rehabilitation/education improves 12-month AF recurrence/burden and health-related quality of life versus standard care in patients undergoing first-time AF ablation</cite>.

# Evidence on symptom burden and quality of life

- Multiple observational and small randomized studies suggest that exercise-based rehabilitation and patient education after AF procedures can improve health-related quality of life and functional capacity, though effects vary by program intensity and adherence. <cite id="39361572">Secondary outcomes in the CREED AF protocol explicitly include health-related quality of life and AF recurrence/burden, reflecting the hypothesis that supervised exercise training and risk-factor modification may improve patient-reported outcomes</cite>.

- Given heterogeneity in program design (e.g., type, intensity, duration, and modality of exercise; inclusion of psychoeducational components), the magnitude and consistency of quality-of-life improvements are variable across studies. Nonetheless, symptom domains such as dyspnea, fatigue, and anxiety often show improvement with structured programs, aligning with broader cardiac rehabilitation benefits in post-procedural AF populations. <cite id="39361572">The trial protocol emphasizes health-related quality of life as a key secondary endpoint, acknowledging patient-reported outcomes as a critical component of post-ablation care</cite>.

# Practical interpretation and gaps

- For recurrence prevention: Current evidence does not conclusively demonstrate that structured CR or exercise-based programs, as stand-alone interventions, reduce AF recurrence after ablation or cardioversion. The most direct comparative trials are still enrolling; results will clarify whether rehabilitation adds incremental benefit beyond antiarrhythmic drug therapy and procedural success. <cite id="39361572">No prior studies have assessed combined prehabilitation/rehabilitation in first-time AF ablation patients, and existing evidence is insufficient to establish a definitive reduction in AF recurrence from such programs</cite>.

- For symptom burden and quality of life: There is more supportive, if heterogeneous, evidence that supervised exercise and comprehensive education can improve functional capacity and quality of life post-procedure. Programs that integrate aerobic/resistive training, rhythm/education sessions, and self-management strategies are most likely to yield clinically meaningful benefits. <cite id="39361572">The CREED AF protocol highlights quality of life as a primary patient-centered outcome, reflecting the clinical rationale that exercise-based rehabilitation may improve patient-reported outcomes after AF ablation</cite>.

# Key ongoing trial (CREED AF)

- Design: Pragmatic randomized controlled trial; 106 adults with paroxysmal/persistent AF scheduled for first-time AF ablation; 1:1 randomization to comprehensive prehabilitation/rehabilitation/education versus standard care; 6-week prehabilitation followed by 6-week rehabilitation; standard care includes a single 30-minute education session. <cite id="39361572">Participants will be randomized 1:1 to the CREED AF intervention (6-week prehabilitation and 6-week rehabilitation with supervised exercise training and risk-factor education/modification) or standard care, with outcomes assessed at baseline, 10 weeks, and 12 months post-ablation</cite>.

Secondary endpoints: health-related quality of life, 12-month AF recurrence/burden (7-day Holter), repeat AF ablation, major adverse cardiovascular events, and cost-effectiveness. <cite id="39361572">The primary outcome is VO2peak by CPET at 10 weeks; secondary outcomes include quality of life, AF recurrence/burden by 7-day Holter, repeat ablation, adverse events, and cost-effectiveness (incremental cost per QALY)</cite>.

- Rationale: Addresses a critical gap by testing whether structured prehabilitation/rehabilitation improves both physiological and patient-centered outcomes after AF ablation. <cite id="39361572">This study aims to assess the clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of comprehensive prehabilitation/rehabilitation/education for first-time AF ablation, with results expected to inform clinical care and future multicenter trials</cite>.

# Clinical takeaway

- If you are counseling patients post-ablation or post-cardioversion, structured CR with supervised exercise and education can plausibly improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, and may reduce recurrence in some cohorts, but definitive, high-quality comparative evidence remains limited. Participation in ongoing or local CR programs is reasonable for symptom improvement and functional recovery, while expectations for recurrence prevention should be tempered until results from contemporary randomized trials (e.g., CREED AF) and meta-analyses are available. <cite id="39361572">There is growing evidence that patient education and exercise-rehabilitation can improve outcomes, but rigorous trials in post-ablation populations are limited; comprehensive prehabilitation/rehabilitation is being tested to determine whether it reduces AF recurrence and improves quality of life compared with standard care</cite>.

<snippet id="33436044">Title: Targeting hypoxic tumor microenvironment in pancreatic cancer.
Authors: Tao, Jinxin, Yang, Gang, Zhou, Wenchuan et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Journal of hematology & oncology
Abstract: Attributable to its late diagnosis, early metastasis, and poor prognosis, pancreatic cancer remains one of the most lethal diseases worldwide. Unlike other solid tumors, pancreatic cancer harbors ample stromal cells and abundant extracellular matrix but lacks vascularization, resulting in persistent and severe hypoxia within the tumor. Hypoxic microenvironment has extensive effects on biological behaviors or malignant phenotypes of pancreatic cancer, including metabolic reprogramming, cancer stemness, invasion and metastasis, and pathological angiogenesis, which synergistically contribute to development and therapeutic resistance of pancreatic cancer. Through various mechanisms including but not confined to maintenance of redox homeostasis, activation of autophagy, epigenetic regulation, and those induced by hypoxia-inducible factors, intratumoral hypoxia drives the above biological processes in pancreatic cancer. Recognizing the pivotal roles of hypoxia in pancreatic cancer progression and therapies, hypoxia-based antitumoral strategies have been continuously developed over the recent years, some of which have been applied in clinical trials to evaluate their efficacy and safety in combinatory therapies for patients with pancreatic cancer. In this review, we discuss the molecular mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced aggressive and therapeutically resistant phenotypes in both pancreatic cancerous and stromal cells. Additionally, we focus more on innovative therapies targeting the tumor hypoxic microenvironment itself, which hold great potential to overcome the resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and to enhance antitumor efficacy and reduce toxicity to normal tissues.</snippet>
<snippet id="34359884">Title: Hypoxia, Metabolic Reprogramming, and Drug Resistance in Liver Cancer.
Authors: Bao, Macus Hao-Ran, Wong, Carmen Chak-Lui | Year: 2021 | Journal: Cells
Abstract: Hypoxia, low oxygen (O 2 ) level, is a hallmark of solid cancers, especially hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), one of the most common and fatal cancers worldwide. Hypoxia contributes to drug resistance in cancer through various molecular mechanisms. In this review, we particularly focus on the roles of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-mediated metabolic reprogramming in drug resistance in HCC. Combination therapies targeting hypoxia-induced metabolic enzymes to overcome drug resistance will also be summarized. Acquisition of drug resistance is the major cause of unsatisfactory clinical outcomes of existing HCC treatments. Extra efforts to identify novel mechanisms to combat refractory hypoxic HCC are warranted for the development of more effective treatment regimens for HCC patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="39804528">Title: Emerging Trends in Neuroblastoma Diagnosis, Therapeutics, and Research.
Authors: Sharma, Rishabh, Yadav, Jaya, Bhat, Sajad Ahmad et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Molecular neurobiology
Abstract: This review explores the current understanding and recent advancements in neuroblastoma, one of the most common extracranial solid pediatric cancers, accounting for ~ 15% of childhood cancer-related mortality. The hallmarks of NBL, including angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis resistance, cell cycle dysregulation, drug resistance, and responses to hypoxia and ROS, underscore its complex biology. The tumor microenvironment's significance in disease progression is acknowledged in this study, along with the pivotal role of cancer stem cells in sustaining tumor growth and heterogeneity. A number of molecular signatures are being studied in order to better understand the disease, with many of them serving as targets for the development of new therapeutics. This includes inhibitor therapies for NBL patients, which notably concentrate on ALK signaling, MDM2, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, Wnt, and RAS-MAPK pathways, along with regulators of epigenetic mechanisms. Additionally, this study offers an extensive understanding of the molecular therapies used, such as monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T therapy, focused on both preclinical and clinical studies. Radiation therapy's evolving role and the promise of stem cell transplantation-mediated interventions underscore the dynamic landscape of NBL treatment. This study has also emphasized the recent progress in the field of diagnosis, encompassing the adoption of artificial intelligence and liquid biopsy as a non-intrusive approach for early detection and ongoing monitoring of NBL. Furthermore, the integration of innovative treatment approaches such as CRISPR-Cas9, and cancer stem cell therapy has also been emphasized in this review.</snippet>
<snippet id="33456577">Title: Cisplatin-resistant NSCLC cells induced by hypoxia transmit resistance to sensitive cells through exosomal PKM2.
Authors: Wang, Dongliang, Zhao, Chaoshuai, Xu, Fei et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Theranostics
Abstract: Hypoxia is commonly observed in solid tumors and contributes to the resistance of DNA damage drugs. However, the mechanisms behind this resistance are still unclear. In this study, we aimed to explore the effects of hypoxia-induced exosomes on non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods: NSCLC cells were subjected to either normoxic or hypoxic conditions to assess cell survival and changes in the expression levels of key proteins. Comparative proteomics were performed to identify exosomal PKM2 in normoxic or hypoxic cisplatin-resistant NSCLC cells-derived exosomes. Functions of hypoxia induced-exosomal PKM2 in promoting cisplatin resistance to NSCLC cells were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo experiments and the molecular mechanisms of hypoxia induced-exosomal PKM2 were demonstrated using flow cytometry, immunoblotting, oxidative stress detection and histological examination. A series of in vitro experiments were performed to evaluate the function of hypoxia-induced exosomes on cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). Results: Hypoxia exacerbated the cisplatin resistance in lung cancer cells due to the increased expression of PKM2 that was observed in the exosomes secreted by hypoxic cisplatin-resistance cells. We identified that hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 transmitted cisplatin-resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells in vitro and in vivo . Mechanistically, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 promoted glycolysis in NSCLC cells to produce reductive metabolites, which may neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by cisplatin. Additionally, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 inhibited apoptosis in a PKM2-BCL2-dependent manner. Moreover, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 reprogrammed CAFs to create an acidic microenvironment promoting NSCLC cells proliferation and cisplatin resistance. Conclusions: Our findings revealed that hypoxia-induced exosomes transmit cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells by delivering PKM2. Exosomal PKM2 may serve as a promising biomarker and therapeutic target for cisplatin resistance in NSCLC.</snippet>
<snippet id="26222076">Title: Mechanisms of Drug Resistance Related to the Microenvironment of Solid Tumors and Possible Strategies to Inhibit Them.
Authors: Tan, Qian, Saggar, Jasdeep K, Yu, Man et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Cancer journal (Sudbury, Mass.)
Abstract: Drug resistance can occur at the individual cellular level or as a result of properties of the tumor microenvironment. The convoluted vasculature within tumors results in robustly proliferating well-nourished cells located proximal to functional blood vessels and regions of slowly proliferating (often hypoxic) cells located distal to functional blood vessels. Irregular blood flow and large distances between functional blood vessels in solid tumors lead to poor drug distribution within them such that cells distal from functional blood vessels are exposed to ineffective concentrations of drug, resulting in therapeutic resistance. Strategies to improve or complement the distribution of anticancer drugs within tumors hold promise for increasing antitumor effects without corresponding increases in normal tissue toxicity. In particular, use of hypoxia-targeted agents and modulation of autophagy have shown promising results in enhancing the distribution of drug activity within solid tumors and hence antitumor efficacy. In this review, we describe causes of resistance to chemotherapy that relate to the microenvironment of solid tumors and the potential to improve antitumor effects by countering such mechanisms of resistance.</snippet>

<snippet id="33278499">Title: Hypoxia-mediated drug resistance in breast cancers.
Authors: McAleese, Courtney E, Choudhury, Chandra, Butcher, Neville J et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Cancer letters
Abstract: Tissue hypoxia in solid tumors is caused by several pathological changes associated with tumor growth, including altered microvasculature structure, increased diffusional distances, and tumor-associated anemia. As the oxygen tension decreases, tumor cells adapt to the limited oxygen supply. Previous studies have shown that such adaptation leads to an aggressive phenotype that is resistant to many anti-cancer therapies. Induction of hypoxia inducible factors (HIFs) mediates many proteomic and genomic changes associated with tumor hypoxia. In breast cancers, HIFs not only predict poor prognosis, but also promote metastasis and drug resistance. Several studies have proposed HIF-1α as a druggable target in drug-resistant breast cancers, leading to the synthesis and development of small molecule inhibitors. Disappointingly, however, none of these small molecule inhibitors have progressed to clinical use. In this review, we briefly discuss the role of HIF-1α in breast cancer drug resistance and summarize the current and future approaches to targeting this transcription factor in breast cancer treatment.</snippet>
<snippet id="29278273">Title: Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) inhibitors from the last decade (2007 to 2016): A "structure-activity relationship" perspective.
Authors: Bhattarai, Deepak, Xu, Xuezhen, Lee, Kyeong | Year: 2018 | Journal: Medicinal research reviews
Abstract: Tumor hypoxia is a common feature in most solid tumors and is associated with overexpression of the hypoxia response pathway. Overexpression of the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1) protein leads to angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis resistance, and many other pro-tumorigenic responses in cancer development. HIF-1 is a promising target in cancer drug development to increase the patient's response to chemotherapy and radiotherapy as well as the survival rate of cancer patients. Since up to 1% of genes are hypoxia-sensitive, a target-specific HIF-1 inhibitor may be a better clinical candidate in cancer drug discovery. Though no HIF-1 inhibitor is clinically available to date, a lot of effort has been applied during the last decade in search of potent HIF-1 inhibitors. In this review, we will summarize the structure-activity relationship of ten different chemotypes reported to be HIF-1 inhibitors in the last decade (2007-2016), their mechanisms of action for HIF-1 inhibition, progress in the way of target-specific inhibitors, and problems associated with current inhibitors. It is anticipated that the results of these research on the medicinal chemistry of HIF-1 inhibitors will provide decent information in the design and development of future inhibitors.</snippet>
<snippet id="17404504">Title: HIF-1-regulated glucose metabolism: a key to apoptosis resistance?
Authors: Fulda, Simone, Debatin, Klaus-Michael | Year: 2007 | Journal: Cell cycle (Georgetown, Tex.)
Abstract: Resistance of human cancers to current treatment regimens remains a challenge in oncology. Therefore, there has been much interest in identifying molecular pathways that are responsible for primary or acquired resistance of cancers. Hypoxia is a characteristic feature of most solid tumors and has been associated with poor treatment response. In response to hypoxia cancer cells undergo a variety of adoptive changes including activation of signaling pathways, which promote cancer cell survival and block cell death. Hypoxia inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) is the major transcription factor that mediates adaptation of cancer cells to the hypoxic environment. There is mounting evidence that Hif-1alpha, the oxygen sensitive subunit of HIF-1, provides protection against cell death and stimulates tumor growth by upregulating genes that are involved in cellular energy metabolism. Thus, Hif-1alpha and hypoxia-inducible genes represent attractive targets for the development of pharmacological inhibitors, which may offer new therapeutic options for a wide range of adult and also pediatric malignancies.</snippet>
<snippet id="23071360">Title: Targeting hypoxia, HIF-1, and tumor glucose metabolism to improve radiotherapy efficacy.
Authors: Meijer, Tineke W H, Kaanders, Johannes H A M, Span, Paul N et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: Radiotherapy, an important treatment modality in oncology, kills cells through induction of oxidative stress. However, malignant tumors vary in their response to irradiation as a consequence of resistance mechanisms taking place at the molecular level. It is important to understand these mechanisms of radioresistance, as counteracting them may improve the efficacy of radiotherapy. In this review, we describe how the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) pathway has a profound effect on the response to radiotherapy. The main focus will be on HIF-1-controlled protection of the vasculature postirradiation and on HIF-1 regulation of glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. This aberrant cellular metabolism increases the antioxidant capacity of tumors, thereby countering the oxidative stress caused by irradiation. From the results of translational studies and the first clinical phase I/II trials, it can be concluded that targeting HIF-1 and tumor glucose metabolism at several levels reduces the antioxidant capacity of tumors, affects the tumor microenvironment, and sensitizes various solid tumors to irradiation.</snippet>

Abstract: Hypoxia is a typical characteristic of most solid malignancies, which has multiple effects on malignant phenotypes and biological behaviors of tumors including epithelial-mesenchymal-transition (EMT), invasion, migration, metastasis, autophagy, stem cell maintenance, pathological angiogenesis, drug resistance, and immunosuppression. <snippet id="27108065">Title: Positive feedback loop between cancer stem cells and angiogenesis in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Authors: Yao, Hong, Liu, Nianli, Lin, Marie C et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Cancer letters
Abstract: Anti-angiogenesis-related therapies have become the standard care for patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as HCC is a highly vascularized solid tumor. Unfortunately, only modest and limited efficacies are observed. Emerging evidence have attributed to the limited efficacy to the presence of cancer stem cells (CSCs) in the tumor. CSCs predominantly drives angiogenesis via releasing proangiogenic factors and exosomes. They have the ability to resistant intratumoral hypoxia via autophagy or by directly forming the tubular structure to obtain blood. On the other hand, the vascular niche in tumor microenvironment also releases growth factors via juxtacrine and paracrine mechanisms to support the growth of CSCs and maintain its stemness features. This positive feedback loop between angiogenesis and CSCs exists in liver tumor microenvironment that is responsible for the development and poor prognosis of HCC. In this review, we summarize recent advances in our understanding of the crosstalks between angiogenesis and CSCs, and their interactions in liver tumor microenvironment and their purpose that an effective anti-angiogenic therapy should also target CSCs for HCC treatment.</snippet>
<snippet id="18855580">Title: Tumour hypoxia affects the responsiveness of cancer cells to chemotherapy and promotes cancer progression.
Authors: Cosse, Jean-Philippe, Michiels, Carine | Year: 2008 | Journal: Anti-cancer agents in medicinal chemistry
Abstract: A solid tumour forms an organ-like structure that is comprised of cancer cells as well as stroma cells (fibroblasts, inflammatory cells) that are embedded in an extracellular matrix and are nourished by vascular network. However, tumoral microenvironment is heterogeneous due to the abnormal vasculature network and high proliferation rate of cancer cells. Because of these features, some regions are starved from oxygen, a phenomenon called hypoxia. Transient hypoxia is associated with inadequate blood flow while chronic hypoxia is the consequence of the increased oxygen diffusion distance due to tumour expansion. Both types of hypoxia are correlated with poor outcome for patients. Moreover, hypoxia also enhances chemoresistance of cancer cells. Firstly, the delivery of drugs in hypoxic area and cellular uptake of it are affected by hypoxia or associated acidity. Secondly, some chemotherapeutic drugs require oxygen to generate free radicals that contribute to cytotoxicity. Last, hypoxia induces cellular adaptations that compromise the effectiveness of chemotherapy. In response to nutrient deprivation due to hypoxia, the rate of proliferation of cancer cells decreases but chemotherapeutic drugs are more effective against proliferating cells. On the other hand, hypoxia induces adaptation by post-translational and transcriptional changes that promote cell survival and resistance to chemotherapy. Through these changes, hypoxia promotes angiogenesis, shift to glycolytic metabolism, expression of ABC transporters, cell survival by inducing the expression of genes encoding growth factors and the modulation of apoptotic process. The aim of this review is to provide a description of known hypoxia-induced mechanisms of chemoresistance at a cellular level.</snippet>

Authors: Tan, Qian, Saggar, Jasdeep K, Yu, Man et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Cancer journal (Sudbury, Mass.)
Abstract: Drug resistance can occur at the individual cellular level or as a result of properties of the tumor microenvironment. The convoluted vasculature within tumors results in robustly proliferating well-nourished cells located proximal to functional blood vessels and regions of slowly proliferating (often hypoxic) cells located distal to functional blood vessels. Irregular blood flow and large distances between functional blood vessels in solid tumors lead to poor drug distribution within them such that cells distal from functional blood vessels are exposed to ineffective concentrations of drug, resulting in therapeutic resistance. Strategies to improve or complement the distribution of anticancer drugs within tumors hold promise for increasing antitumor effects without corresponding increases in normal tissue toxicity. In particular, use of hypoxia-targeted agents and modulation of autophagy have shown promising results in enhancing the distribution of drug activity within solid tumors and hence antitumor efficacy. # Summary

Tumor microenvironment-mediated hypoxia promotes chemotherapy resistance in solid tumors through multiple molecular mechanisms that act at the cellular, intercellular, and vascular levels. These include impaired drug delivery to hypoxic regions, metabolic reprogramming via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), activation of survival pathways and antiapoptotic programs, enhanced detoxification via ABC transporters, induction of autophagy, maintenance of redox homeostasis, epigenetic alterations, and intercellular "resistance spreading" via exosomes. Crosstalk with cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumor vasculature further stabilizes hypoxia and reinforces drug tolerance, leading to treatment failure and poor clinical outcomes.

# Mechanisms by which hypoxia drives chemoresistance

- **Poor drug distribution and direct interference with drug action**: Irregular and convoluted tumor vasculature creates areas distal to functional blood vessels that are chronically hypoxic and receive subtherapeutic drug concentrations. Hypoxia also associates with increased acidity, which can reduce drug uptake and efficacy, and some DNA-damaging agents require oxygen to generate cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), so low oxygen diminishes their direct cytotoxicity. <cite id="26222076">Irregular blood flow and large distances between functional blood vessels in solid tumors lead to poor drug distribution within them such that cells distal from functional blood vessels are exposed to ineffective concentrations of drug, resulting in therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Because of abnormal vasculature and high proliferation, some regions are chronically starved from oxygen; hypoxia affects drug delivery and uptake and impairs oxygen-dependent ROS formation by chemotherapeutics, thereby enhancing resistance.</cite>

- **HIF-mediated transcriptional and metabolic reprogramming**: Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α/2α, which upregulate glycolysis (e.g., HK2, PKM2), lactate export (MCT1/4), and other metabolic genes to sustain energy under low oxygen. This shift reduces reliance on oxidative metabolism and ROS, dampening DNA damage and apoptosis induced by therapies. HIFs also promote stemness, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and pro-survival gene expression, all of which contribute to drug tolerance. <cite id="34359884">Hypoxia contributes to drug resistance in solid cancers via HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming that supports survival under low oxygen and fosters resistance phenotypes.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Through HIF-driven and other mechanisms (redox homeostasis, autophagy, epigenetic regulation), intratumoral hypoxia drives metabolic reprogramming, stemness, invasion, and therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="17404504">HIF-1α protects cancer cells from cell death by upregulating genes involved in cellular energy metabolism, providing a survival advantage under hypoxia and contributing to therapy resistance.</cite>

- **Activation of survival pathways and antiapoptotic programs**: Hypoxia induces expression of survival factors and modulates apoptotic processes, reducing chemotherapy-triggered cell death. HIF-dependent programs suppress oxidative stress and maintain redox balance, directly counteracting the oxidative damage intended by cytotoxic agents. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia maintains redox homeostasis and modulates apoptotic processes, promoting survival under therapy stress.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Hypoxia induces adaptations that promote cell survival, including expression of genes encoding growth factors and modulation of apoptosis, compromising chemotherapy effectiveness.</cite>

- **Enhanced drug efflux and reduced intracellular accumulation**: Hypoxia upregulates ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (e.g., P-gp, BCRP), increasing efflux of chemotherapeutics and reducing their intracellular concentrations below cytotoxic thresholds. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia induces expression of ABC transporters, facilitating drug resistance.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Hypoxia-associated programs include the expression of genes encoding transporters and growth factors that collectively reduce drug effectiveness.</cite>

- **Induction of autophagy for survival under stress**: Hypoxia triggers autophagy, a catabolic process that recycles cytoplasmic contents to generate energy and amino acids, helping cancer cells survive chemotherapy-induced stress and nutrient deprivation. Targeting autophagy can sensitize tumors to chemotherapy in hypoxic settings. <cite id="33436044">Activation of autophagy is a hypoxia-induced mechanism that supports survival and contributes to therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Modulation of autophagy has shown promise in enhancing drug activity in solid tumors by countering hypoxia-driven resistance mechanisms.</cite>

- **Epigenetic alterations and plasticity**: Hypoxia alters chromatin structure and gene expression via HIF-dependent and -independent epigenetic regulators (e.g., histone modifiers and DNA methyltransferases), fostering a transcriptional state compatible with drug tolerance, stemness, and EMT. <cite id="33436044">Epigenetic regulation is a hypoxia-induced mechanism that contributes to aggressive and therapeutically resistant phenotypes.</cite> <cite id="34359884">HIF-mediated metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming under hypoxia supports drug resistance in liver cancer.</cite>

- **Metabolic "neutralization" of therapy-induced ROS**: Hypoxia enhances glycolysis and lactate production, creating a more reducing intracellular milieu that can neutralize ROS generated by chemotherapeutics (e.g., cisplatin), thereby attenuating DNA damage and apoptosis. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 promotes glycolysis and produces reductive metabolites that may neutralize cisplatin-induced ROS, inhibiting apoptosis in a PKM2–BCL2–dependent manner.</cite>

- **Intercellular "resistance spreading" via exosomes and non-cell autonomous effects**: Hypoxic, drug-tolerant or resistant tumor cells secrete exosomes carrying proteins such as PKM2 that transfer resistance traits to neighboring sensitive cells. In NSCLC, hypoxia increases exosomal PKM2, which confers cisplatin resistance by promoting glycolysis, reducing ROS, inhibiting apoptosis, and reprogramming cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to acidify the microenvironment and support proliferation and resistance. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 transmits cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells in vitro and in vivo by promoting glycolysis, neutralizing ROS, inhibiting apoptosis, and reprogramming CAFs to create an acidic microenvironment that fosters resistance.</cite>

- **Stromal and vascular remodeling that sustains hypoxia**: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumor vasculature interact with hypoxic tumor cells to reinforce hypoxic niches. Fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition, angiogenic remodeling, and abnormal vessel maturation create persistent low-oxygen zones that harbor drug-tolerant persister cells. <cite id="33436044">Pancreatic cancer exemplifies how abundant stroma and ECM, combined with poor vascularization, produce persistent hypoxia that drives aggressive behavior and therapeutic resistance via HIF and other mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="27108065">In HCC, cancer stem cells and angiogenesis form a positive feedback loop: CSCs resist hypoxia via autophagy or by forming tubular structures to obtain blood, while vascular niches supply growth factors that maintain stemness, contributing to limited efficacy of anti-angiogenic therapy and poor prognosis.</cite>

# Consequences and clinical implications

- Hypoxia is a hallmark of aggressive solid tumors and is associated with poor prognosis, metastasis, and therapy failure. It fosters a heterogeneous population of drug-tolerant persister cells that outcompete proliferating, drug-sensitive cells once therapy is resumed, leading to relapse. <cite id="34359884">Hypoxia is a hallmark of solid cancers and contributes to drug resistance through HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming, complicating clinical outcomes of existing treatments.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia-driven processes (metabolic reprogramming, stemness, invasion, pathological angiogenesis) synergistically contribute to development and therapeutic resistance.</cite>

- Therapeutic strategies to counter hypoxia-mediated resistance include hypoxia-targeted agents, modulation of autophagy and metabolism, vascular normalization to improve drug delivery, and combination approaches that disrupt HIF-driven survival programs or exosome-mediated resistance transfer. <cite id="26222076">Hypoxia-targeted agents and autophagy modulation can enhance drug distribution and activity in solid tumors, improving antitumor efficacy.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Innovative therapies targeting the hypoxic tumor microenvironment aim to overcome resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and enhance antitumor efficacy while reducing toxicity.</cite>

# Key molecular pathways and nodes

- **HIF-1α/2α**: Central drivers of hypoxia responses that reprogram metabolism, promote stemness, and induce survival and antiapoptotic genes, thereby reducing chemotherapy effectiveness. <cite id="34359884">HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming underlies hypoxia-driven drug resistance in liver cancer.</cite> <cite id="17404504">HIF-1α upregulates energy metabolism genes to protect cancer cells from death, contributing to therapy resistance.</cite>

- **Glycolysis and lactate metabolism (PKM2, HK2, MCT1/4)**: Hypoxia enhances glycolysis and lactate export, generating a reducing environment that neutralizes therapy-induced ROS and supports survival. <cite id="33456577">Exosomal PKM2 promotes glycolysis and reductive metabolite production that neutralize cisplatin-induced ROS, reducing apoptosis.</cite>

- **Autophagy and redox homeostasis**: Hypoxia activates autophagy and antioxidant defenses, enabling survival under chemotherapy-induced stress and limiting DNA damage. <cite id="33436044">Activation of autophagy and maintenance of redox homeostasis are hypoxia-induced mechanisms that promote resistance.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Modulating autophagy can counter hypoxia-driven resistance and improve drug activity.</cite>

- **ABC transporters and drug efflux**: Hypoxia upregulates drug efflux pumps, lowering intracellular drug levels. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia induces ABC transporter expression, facilitating drug resistance.</cite>

- **Epigenetic regulation**: Hypoxia-driven epigenetic changes sustain transcriptional programs compatible with drug tolerance and plasticity. <cite id="33436044">Epigenetic regulation is a hypoxia-induced mechanism contributing to resistant phenotypes.</cite>

- **Intercellular communication via exosomes**: Transfer of resistance determinants (e.g., PKM2) from hypoxic, resistant cells to neighboring or distant cells can convert a population of sensitive cells into resistant ones, accelerating tumor adaptation. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 confers cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells and reprograms CAFs to acidify the microenvironment, promoting proliferation and resistance.</cite>

# Take-home message

Hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment is not merely a passive feature but an active driver of chemoresistance through coordinated metabolic, signaling, epigenetic, and intercellular mechanisms. Addressing hypoxia by targeting HIF-driven programs, metabolic rewiring, autophagy, drug efflux, and hypoxia-facilitated intercellular communication, as well as improving oxygen and drug delivery to hypoxic regions, are promising strategies to sensitize solid tumors to chemotherapy and improve patient outcomes. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia-based strategies targeting the hypoxic microenvironment hold potential to overcome resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and enhance antitumor efficacy.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Countering hypoxia-related mechanisms of resistance—such as impaired drug distribution, autophagy, and metabolic reprogramming—can increase antitumor effects without increasing normal-tissue toxicity.</cite>
