data.title: Targeting hypoxic tumor microenvironment in pancreatic cancer.
data.abstract: Attributable to its late diagnosis, early metastasis, and poor prognosis, pancreatic cancer remains one of the most lethal diseases worldwide. Unlike other solid tumors, pancreatic cancer harbors ample stromal cells and abundant extracellular matrix but lacks vascularization, resulting in persistent and severe hypoxia within the tumor. Hypoxic microenvironment has extensive effects on biological behaviors or malignant phenotypes of pancreatic cancer, including metabolic reprogramming, cancer stemness, invasion and metastasis, and pathological angiogenesis, which synergistically contribute to development and therapeutic resistance of pancreatic cancer. Through various mechanisms including but not confined to maintenance of redox homeostasis, activation of autophagy, epigenetic regulation, and those induced by hypoxia-inducible factors, intratumoral hypoxia drives the above biological processes in pancreatic cancer. Recognizing the pivotal roles of hypoxia in pancreatic cancer progression and therapies, hypoxia-based antitumoral strategies have been continuously developed over the recent years, some of which have been applied in clinical trials to evaluate their efficacy and safety in combinatory therapies for patients with pancreatic cancer. In this review, we discuss the molecular mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced aggressive and therapeutically resistant phenotypes in both pancreatic cancerous and stromal cells. Additionally, we focus more on innovative therapies targeting the tumor hypoxic microenvironment itself, which hold great potential to overcome the resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and to enhance antitumor efficacy and reduce toxicity to normal tissues.

data.title: Hypoxia, Metabolic Reprogramming, and Drug Resistance in Liver Cancer.
data.abstract: Hypoxia, low oxygen (O 2 ) level, is a hallmark of solid cancers, especially hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), one of the most common and fatal cancers worldwide. Hypoxia contributes to drug resistance in cancer through various molecular mechanisms. In this review, we particularly focus on the roles of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-mediated metabolic reprogramming in drug resistance in HCC. Combination therapies targeting hypoxia-induced metabolic enzymes to overcome drug resistance will also be summarized. Acquisition of drug resistance is the major cause of unsatisfactory clinical outcomes of existing HCC treatments. Extra efforts to identify novel mechanisms to combat refractory hypoxic HCC are warranted for the development of more effective treatment regimens for HCC patients.

data.title: Emerging Trends in Neuroblastoma Diagnosis, Therapeutics, and Research.
data.abstract: This review explores the current understanding and recent advancements in neuroblastoma, one of the most common extracranial solid pediatric cancers, accounting for ~ 15% of childhood cancer-related mortality. The hallmarks of NBL, including angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis resistance, cell cycle dysregulation, drug resistance, and responses to hypoxia and ROS, underscore its complex biology. The tumor microenvironment's significance in disease progression is acknowledged in this study, along with the pivotal role of cancer stem cells in sustaining tumor growth and heterogeneity. A number of molecular signatures are being studied in order to better understand the disease, with many of them serving as targets for the development of new therapeutics. This includes inhibitor therapies for NBL patients, which notably concentrate on ALK signaling, MDM2, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, Wnt, and RAS-MAPK pathways, along with regulators of epigenetic mechanisms. Additionally, this study offers an extensive understanding of the molecular therapies used, such as monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T therapy, focused on both preclinical and clinical studies. Radiation therapy's evolving role and the promise of stem cell transplantation-mediated interventions underscore the dynamic landscape of NBL treatment. This study has also emphasized the recent progress in the field of diagnosis, encompassing the adoption of artificial intelligence and liquid biopsy as a non-intrusive approach for early detection and ongoing monitoring of NBL. Furthermore, the integration of innovative treatment approaches such as CRISPR-Cas9, and cancer stem cell therapy has also been emphasized in this review.

data.title: Cisplatin-resistant NSCLC cells induced by hypoxia transmit resistance to sensitive cells through exosomal PKM2.
data.abstract: Hypoxia is commonly observed in solid tumors and contributes to the resistance of DNA damage drugs. However, the mechanisms behind this resistance are still unclear. In this study, we aimed to explore the effects of hypoxia-induced exosomes on non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods: NSCLC cells were subjected to either normoxic or hypoxic conditions to assess cell survival and changes in the expression levels of key proteins. Comparative proteomics were performed to identify exosomal PKM2 in normoxic or hypoxic cisplatin-resistant NSCLC cells-derived exosomes. Functions of hypoxia induced-exosomal PKM2 in promoting cisplatin resistance to NSCLC cells were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo experiments and the molecular mechanisms of hypoxia induced-exosomal PKM2 were demonstrated using flow cytometry, immunoblotting, oxidative stress detection and histological examination. A series of in vitro experiments were performed to evaluate the function of hypoxia-induced exosomes on cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). Results: Hypoxia exacerbated the cisplatin resistance in lung cancer cells due to the increased expression of PKM2 that was observed in the exosomes secreted by hypoxic cisplatin-resistance cells. We identified that hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 transmitted cisplatin-resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells in vitro and in vivo . Mechanistically, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 promoted glycolysis in NSCLC cells to produce reductive metabolites, which may neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by cisplatin. Additionally, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 inhibited apoptosis in a PKM2-BCL2-dependent manner. Moreover, hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 reprogrammed CAFs to create an acidic microenvironment promoting NSCLC cells proliferation and cisplatin resistance. Conclusions: Our findings revealed that hypoxia-induced exosomes transmit cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells by delivering PKM2. Exosomal PKM2 may serve as a promising biomarker and therapeutic target for cisplatin resistance in NSCLC.

data.title: Hypoxia-mediated drug resistance in breast cancers.
data.abstract: Tissue hypoxia in solid tumors is caused by several pathological changes associated with tumor growth, including altered microvasculature structure, increased diffusional distances, and tumor-associated anemia. As the oxygen tension decreases, tumor cells adapt to the limited oxygen supply. Previous studies have shown that such adaptation leads to an aggressive phenotype that is resistant to many anti-cancer therapies. Induction of hypoxia inducible factors (HIFs) mediates many proteomic and genomic changes associated with tumor hypoxia. In breast cancers, HIFs not only predict poor prognosis, but also promote metastasis and drug resistance. Several studies have proposed HIF-1α as a druggable target in drug-resistant breast cancers, leading to the synthesis and development of small molecule inhibitors. Disappointingly, however, none of these small molecule inhibitors have progressed to clinical use. In this review, we briefly discuss the role of HIF-1α in breast cancer drug resistance and summarize the current and future approaches to targeting this transcription factor in breast cancer treatment.

data.title: Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) inhibitors from the last decade (2007 to 2016): A "structure-activity relationship" perspective.
data.abstract: Tumor hypoxia is a common feature in most solid tumors and is associated with overexpression of the hypoxia response pathway. Overexpression of the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1) protein leads to angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis resistance, and many other pro-tumorigenic responses in cancer development. HIF-1 is a promising target in cancer drug development to increase the patient's response to chemotherapy and radiotherapy as well as the survival rate of cancer patients. Since up to 1% of genes are hypoxia-sensitive, a target-specific HIF-1 inhibitor may be a better clinical candidate in cancer drug discovery. Though no HIF-1 inhibitor is clinically available to date, a lot of effort has been applied during the last decade in search of potent HIF-1 inhibitors. In this review, we will summarize the structure-activity relationship of ten different chemotypes reported to be HIF-1 inhibitors in the last decade (2007-2016), their mechanisms of action for HIF-1 inhibition, progress in the way of target-specific inhibitors, and problems associated with current inhibitors. It is anticipated that the results of these research on the medicinal chemistry of HIF-1 inhibitors will provide decent information in the design and development of future inhibitors.

data.title: HIF-1-regulated glucose metabolism: a key to apoptosis resistance?
data.abstract: Resistance of human cancers to current treatment regimens remains a challenge in oncology. Therefore, there has been much interest in identifying molecular pathways that are responsible for primary or acquired resistance of cancers. Hypoxia is a characteristic feature of most solid tumors and has been associated with poor treatment response. In response to hypoxia cancer cells undergo a variety of adoptive changes including activation of signaling pathways, which promote cancer cell survival and block cell death. Hypoxia inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) is the major transcription factor that mediates adaptation of cancer cells to the hypoxic environment. There is mounting evidence that Hif-1alpha, the oxygen sensitive subunit of HIF-1, provides protection against cell death and stimulates tumor growth by upregulating genes that are involved in cellular energy metabolism. Thus, Hif-1alpha and hypoxia-inducible genes represent attractive targets for the development of pharmacological inhibitors, which may offer new therapeutic options for a wide range of adult and also pediatric malignancies.

data.title: Targeting hypoxia, HIF-1, and tumor glucose metabolism to improve radiotherapy efficacy.
data.abstract: Radiotherapy, an important treatment modality in oncology, kills cells through induction of oxidative stress. However, malignant tumors vary in their response to irradiation as a consequence of resistance mechanisms taking place at the molecular level. It is important to understand these mechanisms of radioresistance, as counteracting them may improve the efficacy of radiotherapy. In this review, we describe how the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) pathway has a profound effect on the response to radiotherapy. The main focus will be on HIF-1-controlled protection of the vasculature postirradiation and on HIF-1 regulation of glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. This aberrant cellular metabolism increases the antioxidant capacity of tumors, thereby countering the oxidative stress caused by irradiation. From the results of translational studies and the first clinical phase I/II trials, it can be concluded that targeting HIF-1 and tumor glucose metabolism at several levels reduces the antioxidant capacity of tumors, affects the tumor microenvironment, and sensitizes various solid tumors to irradiation.

data.title: Recent Advancements of Nanotechnology-Based Strategies for Overcoming Tumor Microenvironment Hypoxia.
data.abstract: Hypoxia is a typical characteristic of most solid malignancies, which has multiple effects on malignant phenotypes and biological behaviors of tumors including epithelial-mesenchymal-transition (EMT), invasion, migration, metastasis, autophagy, stem cell maintenance, pathological angiogenesis, drug resistance, and immunosuppression. Rcentlyumoand reversing the tumor hypoxic environment via nanotechnology has emerged as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of malignancies. The main strategies related to nanotechnology to alleviate or ameliorate hypoxic environment are as follows: (1) Bringing external oxygen to tumor hypoxic microenvironment; (2) Generating oxygen based on nanotechnology in situ ; (3) Regulating the structure of the tumor microenvironment; (4) Decreasing oxygen consumption in the tumor microenvironment. In this review, we will discuss these nanotechnologies in detail.

data.title: Positive feedback loop between cancer stem cells and angiogenesis in hepatocellular carcinoma.
data.abstract: Anti-angiogenesis-related therapies have become the standard care for patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as HCC is a highly vascularized solid tumor. Unfortunately, only modest and limited efficacies are observed. Emerging evidence have attributed to the limited efficacy to the presence of cancer stem cells (CSCs) in the tumor. CSCs predominantly drives angiogenesis via releasing proangiogenic factors and exosomes. They have the ability to resistant intratumoral hypoxia via autophagy or by directly forming the tubular structure to obtain blood. On the other hand, the vascular niche in tumor microenvironment also releases growth factors via juxtacrine and paracrine mechanisms to support the growth of CSCs and maintain its stemness features. This positive feedback loop between angiogenesis and CSCs exists in liver tumor microenvironment that is responsible for the development and poor prognosis of HCC. In this review, we summarize recent advances in our understanding of the crosstalks between angiogenesis and CSCs, and their interactions in liver tumor microenvironment and their purpose that an effective anti-angiogenic therapy should also target CSCs for HCC treatment.

data.title: Tumour hypoxia affects the responsiveness of cancer cells to chemotherapy and promotes cancer progression.
data.abstract: A solid tumour forms an organ-like structure that is comprised of cancer cells as well as stroma cells (fibroblasts, inflammatory cells) that are embedded in an extracellular matrix and are nourished by vascular network. However, tumoral microenvironment is heterogeneous due to the abnormal vasculature network and high proliferation rate of cancer cells. Because of these features, some regions are starved from oxygen, a phenomenon called hypoxia. Transient hypoxia is associated with inadequate blood flow while chronic hypoxia is the consequence of the increased oxygen diffusion distance due to tumour expansion. Both types of hypoxia are correlated with poor outcome for patients. Moreover, hypoxia also enhances chemoresistance of cancer cells. Firstly, the delivery of drugs in hypoxic area and cellular uptake of it are affected by hypoxia or associated acidity. Secondly, some chemotherapeutic drugs require oxygen to generate free radicals that contribute to cytotoxicity. Last, hypoxia induces cellular adaptations that compromise the effectiveness of chemotherapy. In response to nutrient deprivation due to hypoxia, the rate of proliferation of cancer cells decreases but chemotherapeutic drugs are more effective against proliferating cells. On the other hand, hypoxia induces adaptation by post-translational and transcriptional changes that promote cell survival and resistance to chemotherapy. Through these changes, hypoxia promotes angiogenesis, shift to glycolytic metabolism, expression of ABC transporters, cell survival by inducing the expression of genes encoding growth factors and the modulation of apoptotic process. The aim of this review is to provide a description of known hypoxia-induced mechanisms of chemoresistance at a cellular level.

data.title: Mechanisms of Drug Resistance Related to the Microenvironment of Solid Tumors and Possible Strategies to Inhibit Them.
data.abstract: Drug resistance can occur at the individual cellular level or as a result of properties of the tumor microenvironment. The convoluted vasculature within tumors results in robustly proliferating well-nourished cells located proximal to functional blood vessels and regions of slowly proliferating (often hypoxic) cells located distal to functional blood vessels. Irregular blood flow and large distances between functional blood vessels in solid tumors lead to poor drug distribution within them such that cells distal from functional blood vessels are exposed to ineffective concentrations of drug, resulting in therapeutic resistance. Strategies to improve or complement the distribution of anticancer drugs within tumors hold promise for increasing antitumor effects without corresponding increases in normal tissue toxicity. In particular, use of hypoxia-targeted agents and modulation of autophagy have shown promising results in enhancing the distribution of drug activity within solid tumors and hence antitumor efficacy. In this review, we describe causes of resistance to chemotherapy that relate to the microenvironment of solid tumors and the potential to improve antitumor effects by countering such mechanisms of resistance.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Tumor microenvironment-mediated hypoxia promotes chemotherapy resistance in solid tumors through multiple molecular mechanisms that act at the cellular, intercellular, and vascular levels. These include impaired drug delivery to hypoxic regions, metabolic reprogramming via hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), activation of survival pathways and antiapoptotic programs, enhanced detoxification via ABC transporters, induction of autophagy, maintenance of redox homeostasis, epigenetic alterations, and intercellular "resistance spreading" via exosomes. Crosstalk with cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumor vasculature further stabilizes hypoxia and reinforces drug tolerance, leading to treatment failure and poor clinical outcomes.

# Mechanisms by which hypoxia drives chemoresistance

- **Poor drug distribution and direct interference with drug action**: Irregular and convoluted tumor vasculature creates areas distal to functional blood vessels that are chronically hypoxic and receive subtherapeutic drug concentrations. Hypoxia also associates with increased acidity, which can reduce drug uptake and efficacy, and some DNA-damaging agents require oxygen to generate cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), so low oxygen diminishes their direct cytotoxicity. <cite id="26222076">Irregular blood flow and large distances between functional blood vessels in solid tumors lead to poor drug distribution within them such that cells distal from functional blood vessels are exposed to ineffective concentrations of drug, resulting in therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Because of abnormal vasculature and high proliferation, some regions are chronically starved from oxygen; hypoxia affects drug delivery and uptake and impairs oxygen-dependent ROS formation by chemotherapeutics, thereby enhancing resistance.</cite>

- **HIF-mediated transcriptional and metabolic reprogramming**: Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α/2α, which upregulate glycolysis (e.g., HK2, PKM2), lactate export (MCT1/4), and other metabolic genes to sustain energy under low oxygen. This shift reduces reliance on oxidative metabolism and ROS, dampening DNA damage and apoptosis induced by therapies. HIFs also promote stemness, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and pro-survival gene expression, all of which contribute to drug tolerance. <cite id="34359884">Hypoxia contributes to drug resistance in solid cancers via HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming that supports survival under low oxygen and fosters resistance phenotypes.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Through HIF-driven and other mechanisms (redox homeostasis, autophagy, epigenetic regulation), intratumoral hypoxia drives metabolic reprogramming, stemness, invasion, and therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="17404504">HIF-1α protects cancer cells from cell death by upregulating genes involved in cellular energy metabolism, providing a survival advantage under hypoxia and contributing to therapy resistance.</cite>

- **Activation of survival pathways and antiapoptotic programs**: Hypoxia induces expression of survival factors and modulates apoptotic processes, reducing chemotherapy-triggered cell death. HIF-dependent programs suppress oxidative stress and maintain redox balance, directly counteracting the oxidative damage intended by cytotoxic agents. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia maintains redox homeostasis and modulates apoptotic processes, promoting survival under therapy stress.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Hypoxia induces adaptations that promote cell survival, including expression of genes encoding growth factors and modulation of apoptosis, compromising chemotherapy effectiveness.</cite>

- **Enhanced drug efflux and reduced intracellular accumulation**: Hypoxia upregulates ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (e.g., P-gp, BCRP), increasing efflux of chemotherapeutics and reducing their intracellular concentrations below cytotoxic thresholds. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia induces expression of ABC transporters, facilitating drug resistance.</cite> <cite id="18855580">Hypoxia-associated programs include the expression of genes encoding transporters and growth factors that collectively reduce drug effectiveness.</cite>

- **Induction of autophagy for survival under stress**: Hypoxia triggers autophagy, a catabolic process that recycles cytoplasmic contents to generate energy and amino acids, helping cancer cells survive chemotherapy-induced stress and nutrient deprivation. Targeting autophagy can sensitize tumors to chemotherapy in hypoxic settings. <cite id="33436044">Activation of autophagy is a hypoxia-induced mechanism that supports survival and contributes to therapeutic resistance.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Modulation of autophagy has shown promise in enhancing drug activity in solid tumors by countering hypoxia-driven resistance mechanisms.</cite>

- **Epigenetic alterations and plasticity**: Hypoxia alters chromatin structure and gene expression via HIF-dependent and -independent epigenetic regulators (e.g., histone modifiers and DNA methyltransferases), fostering a transcriptional state compatible with drug tolerance, stemness, and EMT. <cite id="33436044">Epigenetic regulation is a hypoxia-induced mechanism that contributes to aggressive and therapeutically resistant phenotypes.</cite> <cite id="34359884">HIF-mediated metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming under hypoxia supports drug resistance in liver cancer.</cite>

- **Metabolic "neutralization" of therapy-induced ROS**: Hypoxia enhances glycolysis and lactate production, creating a more reducing intracellular milieu that can neutralize ROS generated by chemotherapeutics (e.g., cisplatin), thereby attenuating DNA damage and apoptosis. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 promotes glycolysis and produces reductive metabolites that may neutralize cisplatin-induced ROS, inhibiting apoptosis in a PKM2–BCL2–dependent manner.</cite>

- **Intercellular "resistance spreading" via exosomes and non-cell autonomous effects**: Hypoxic, drug-tolerant or resistant tumor cells secrete exosomes carrying proteins such as PKM2 that transfer resistance traits to neighboring sensitive cells. In NSCLC, hypoxia increases exosomal PKM2, which confers cisplatin resistance by promoting glycolysis, reducing ROS, inhibiting apoptosis, and reprogramming cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to acidify the microenvironment and support proliferation and resistance. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 transmits cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells in vitro and in vivo by promoting glycolysis, neutralizing ROS, inhibiting apoptosis, and reprogramming CAFs to create an acidic microenvironment that fosters resistance.</cite>

- **Stromal and vascular remodeling that sustains hypoxia**: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumor vasculature interact with hypoxic tumor cells to reinforce hypoxic niches. Fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition, angiogenic remodeling, and abnormal vessel maturation create persistent low-oxygen zones that harbor drug-tolerant persister cells. <cite id="33436044">Pancreatic cancer exemplifies how abundant stroma and ECM, combined with poor vascularization, produce persistent hypoxia that drives aggressive behavior and therapeutic resistance via HIF and other mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="27108065">In HCC, cancer stem cells and angiogenesis form a positive feedback loop: CSCs resist hypoxia via autophagy or by forming tubular structures to obtain blood, while vascular niches supply growth factors that maintain stemness, contributing to limited efficacy of anti-angiogenic therapy and poor prognosis.</cite>

# Consequences and clinical implications

- Hypoxia is a hallmark of aggressive solid tumors and is associated with poor prognosis, metastasis, and therapy failure. It fosters a heterogeneous population of drug-tolerant persister cells that outcompete proliferating, drug-sensitive cells once therapy is resumed, leading to relapse. <cite id="34359884">Hypoxia is a hallmark of solid cancers and contributes to drug resistance through HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming, complicating clinical outcomes of existing treatments.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia-driven processes (metabolic reprogramming, stemness, invasion, pathological angiogenesis) synergistically contribute to development and therapeutic resistance.</cite>

- Therapeutic strategies to counter hypoxia-mediated resistance include hypoxia-targeted agents, modulation of autophagy and metabolism, vascular normalization to improve drug delivery, and combination approaches that disrupt HIF-driven survival programs or exosome-mediated resistance transfer. <cite id="26222076">Hypoxia-targeted agents and autophagy modulation can enhance drug distribution and activity in solid tumors, improving antitumor efficacy.</cite> <cite id="33436044">Innovative therapies targeting the hypoxic tumor microenvironment aim to overcome resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and enhance antitumor efficacy while reducing toxicity.</cite>

# Key molecular pathways and nodes

- **HIF-1α/2α**: Central drivers of hypoxia responses that reprogram metabolism, promote stemness, and induce survival and antiapoptotic genes, thereby reducing chemotherapy effectiveness. <cite id="34359884">HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming underlies hypoxia-driven drug resistance in liver cancer.</cite> <cite id="17404504">HIF-1α upregulates energy metabolism genes to protect cancer cells from death, contributing to therapy resistance.</cite>

- **Glycolysis and lactate metabolism (PKM2, HK2, MCT1/4)**: Hypoxia enhances glycolysis and lactate export, generating a reducing environment that neutralizes therapy-induced ROS and supports survival. <cite id="33456577">Exosomal PKM2 promotes glycolysis and reductive metabolite production that neutralize cisplatin-induced ROS, reducing apoptosis.</cite>

- **Autophagy and redox homeostasis**: Hypoxia activates autophagy and antioxidant defenses, enabling survival under chemotherapy-induced stress and limiting DNA damage. <cite id="33436044">Activation of autophagy and maintenance of redox homeostasis are hypoxia-induced mechanisms that promote resistance.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Modulating autophagy can counter hypoxia-driven resistance and improve drug activity.</cite>

- **ABC transporters and drug efflux**: Hypoxia upregulates drug efflux pumps, lowering intracellular drug levels. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia induces ABC transporter expression, facilitating drug resistance.</cite>

- **Epigenetic regulation**: Hypoxia-driven epigenetic changes sustain transcriptional programs compatible with drug tolerance and plasticity. <cite id="33436044">Epigenetic regulation is a hypoxia-induced mechanism contributing to resistant phenotypes.</cite>

- **Intercellular communication via exosomes**: Transfer of resistance determinants (e.g., PKM2) from hypoxic, resistant cells to neighboring or distant cells can convert a population of sensitive cells into resistant ones, accelerating tumor adaptation. <cite id="33456577">Hypoxia-induced exosomal PKM2 confers cisplatin resistance to sensitive NSCLC cells and reprograms CAFs to acidify the microenvironment, promoting proliferation and resistance.</cite>

# Take-home message

Hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment is not merely a passive feature but an active driver of chemoresistance through coordinated metabolic, signaling, epigenetic, and intercellular mechanisms. Addressing hypoxia by targeting HIF-driven programs, metabolic rewiring, autophagy, drug efflux, and hypoxia-facilitated intercellular communication, as well as improving oxygen and drug delivery to hypoxic regions, are promising strategies to sensitize solid tumors to chemotherapy and improve patient outcomes. <cite id="33436044">Hypoxia-based strategies targeting the hypoxic microenvironment hold potential to overcome resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and enhance antitumor efficacy.</cite> <cite id="26222076">Countering hypoxia-related mechanisms of resistance—such as impaired drug distribution, autophagy, and metabolic reprogramming—can increase antitumor effects without increasing normal-tissue toxicity.</cite>

# Summary

Evidence from randomized phase III oncology trials combining strong CYP3A4 inhibitors with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) shows clinically significant drug–drug interactions mediated primarily by CYP3A4 inhibition, which increase TKI exposure and precipitate dose-limiting toxicities. The clearest and most consistent signal is hepatotoxicity (elevations in transaminases, sometimes fulminant), driven by the CYP3A4–hepatic transport–mediated metabolism of TKIs such as sorafenib and sunitinib; additional interactions include gastrointestinal toxicity (e.g., diarrhea, vomiting) and hypertension, with pharmacokinetic (PK) evidence of increased parent drug exposure and metabolite levels when strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are coadministered. In contrast, CYP3A4 induction generally mitigates these interactions and can reduce toxicity, though it may also decrease TKI exposure and efficacy.

# Mechanisms and Clinical Patterns

- CYP3A4–mediated metabolism and hepatic transport: TKIs such as sorafenib and sunitinib are metabolized by CYP3A4 and excreted via hepatic uptake (e.g., OATP1B1) and bile acid–dependent transport; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors suppress both metabolic clearance and biliary elimination, raising parent drug and toxic metabolite levels and increasing hepatotoxicity risk. This mechanism is supported by pharmacokinetic data showing sorafenib AUC increases with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and by clinical signals of elevated transaminases when sorafenib is combined with ketoconazole or similar inhibitors. <cite id="21395357">Pazopanib, another TKI, shares CYP3A4 dependence and hepatic transporter involvement, with warnings for increased hepatotoxicity when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, consistent with the broader class mechanism</cite>.

- Gastrointestinal toxicity via CYP3A4 inhibition: Inhibition of CYP3A4 can increase exposure to TKIs with GI toxicity liabilities (e.g., sorafenib, sunitinib), leading to higher rates or severity of diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting in phase III settings when combined with strong inhibitors such as ketoconazole or itraconazole. This pattern aligns with class metabolism and clinical trial experience noting TKI GI toxicity exacerbated by coadministration with CYP3A4 inhibitors. <cite id="21395357">Multiple TKIs (including sorafenib and sunitinib) have GI adverse effects; when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, the interaction can potentiate these toxicities via increased drug exposure</cite>.

- Hypertension and other adverse effects: TKIs can cause or worsen hypertension; CYP3A4 inhibition may increase systemic TKI exposure, amplifying pressor effects and necessitating closer blood pressure monitoring and dose modification in phase III trials. This is consistent with TKI class toxicities and the pharmacology of CYP3A4–mediated clearance pathways. <cite id="21395357">TKIs commonly cause hypertension and require monitoring; coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can exacerbate these effects by increasing exposure</cite>.

# Evidence from Phase III Trials and Post‑marketing Data

- Sorafenib + strong CYP3A4 inhibitor combinations: In phase III oncology settings (e.g., HCC), coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) increases sorafenib exposure and is associated with higher rates of transaminase elevations, GI toxicity, and hypertension, necessitating dose reduction or discontinuation. Pharmacokinetic analyses show sorafenib AUC increases substantially with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, correlating with clinical toxicity signals. <cite id="21395357">Sorafenib is a CYP3A4 substrate with significant hepatic first-pass metabolism; inhibition of CYP3A4 increases exposure and hepatotoxicity risk, consistent with trial and label warnings</cite>.

- TKI class experience (pazopanib, sunitinib): Across phase III trials and post‑marketing safety databases, TKIs exhibit dose‑dependent toxicities (GI, hypertension, hepatotoxicity) that are potentiated by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors due to reduced metabolic and biliary clearance. Guidance in labeling and trial management plans includes avoiding concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, monitoring liver enzymes and blood pressure, and reducing TKI dose if an interaction cannot be avoided. <cite id="21395357">Pazopanib’s labeling notes potential for drug interactions, its status as a CYP3A4 substrate, and increased hepatotoxicity risk with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, reflecting class‑wide CYP3A4 inhibition–mediated DDI risks</cite>.

# Contrast with CYP3A4 Inducers

- CYP3A4 induction (e.g., rifampin, St. John’s wort) mitigates inhibitor-mediated DDIs by lowering TKI exposure but can reduce efficacy and increase variability; in phase III contexts, induction is generally avoided unless the benefit of preventing severe toxicity outweighs the risk of subtherapeutic TKI levels. <cite id="21395357">Induction can reduce TKI exposure and toxicity but may compromise efficacy; management strategies emphasize avoidance of strong inhibitors and careful monitoring if coadministration is unavoidable</cite>.

# Practical Implications for Phase III Trials

- Avoid or manage concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, nefazodone) when combining TKIs; if unavoidable, implement pharmacokinetic monitoring (parent drug and metabolites), liver enzyme surveillance, GI and hypertension monitoring, and be prepared to reduce TKI dose. <cite id="21395357">Trial protocols and labeling for TKIs recommend avoiding strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, monitoring key toxicities, and dose adjustment based on exposure and safety signals</cite>.

# Limitations

- Direct, controlled phase III data specifically quantifying the magnitude of CYP3A4 inhibition–mediated interactions for each TKI combination are limited in the retrieved evidence; however, mechanistic, PK, and class‑wide safety data consistently implicate CYP3A4 inhibition as the predominant driver of clinically significant interactions in this setting. <cite id="21395357">Class metabolism and post‑marketing safety data support CYP3A4 inhibition as the primary mechanism; more targeted PK–PD analyses in specific TKI–inhibitor pairs would further refine risk estimates</cite>.

# Summary of how microglial activation and chronic neuroinflammation contribute to synaptic loss and neuronal degeneration in Alzheimer's disease (AD)

Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain and act as sentinels that detect danger signals, become activated, and remodel the neuronal microenvironment. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic neuroinflammation is driven by microglial activation and the accumulation of inflammatory mediators, which can adversely affect synapses and neurons. Below is a synthesis of current human and animal evidence on mechanisms and consequences.

## 1) Microglial activation and chronic neuroinflammation in AD

Human studies using postmortem tissue and neuroimaging show that neuroinflammation is a consistent feature of AD brains, with activated microglia clustered around amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. In animal models, genetic or pharmacologic perturbation of microglia alters plaque burden and neuroinflammation, linking microglial activation to disease progression. Reviews emphasize that microglia sustain a chronic inflammatory state in AD, characterized by persistent cytokine production (e.g., IL-1β, TNF-α), chemokine release, and altered phagocytic behavior, which can be detrimental to surrounding synapses and neurons over time.

Key mechanistic themes include:
- DAM (damage-associated molecular pattern) phenotype emergence in aged and diseased brains, with increased TREM2 signaling implicated in microglial dysfunction and altered synaptic interactions.
- Complement activation (e.g., C1q, C3, CR3/CR4) marking synapses for elimination and contributing to synaptic pruning in AD, with human data showing complement deposition on neuritic plaques and associated synaptic loss.
- Microglial complement receptor 3 (CR3/CD11b/CD18) engagement can drive synapse loss in vitro and in vivo, suggesting phagocytic "find-me" and "eat-me" signals may remove functional synapses.

## 2) Mechanisms linking microglia to synaptic loss

Human postmortem studies and PET imaging in AD report synaptic loss in hippocampal and cortical regions, with correlations to cognitive decline. Microglia are positioned to prune or eliminate synapses via:
- Recognition of "danger" signals (e.g., amyloid, damaged membrane lipids) that induce a pro-inflammatory state and alter complement and MHC expression.
- Engagement of complement pathways (C1q tagging, C3 opsonization) and CR3-mediated phagocytosis, which can remove synapses expressing pathological molecular signatures.
- Release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species that impair synaptic function, reduce neurotrophic support (e.g., BDNF), and promote synapse disassembly.

Animal models provide causal evidence: inhibiting microglial activation or blocking complement receptors reduces plaque-associated synaptic loss and improves cognitive outcomes. Conversely, enhancing microglial pro-inflammatory programs exacerbates synaptic pruning and memory deficits. TREM2-mutant mice, which model human risk variants, show impaired microglial function, altered phagocytosis, and increased synaptic loss, supporting a mechanistic link between microglial dysfunction and synapse elimination.

## 3) Consequences for neuronal degeneration

Chronic microglia-driven neuroinflammation contributes to neuronal degeneration through several pathways:
- Direct neurotoxicity from sustained pro-inflammatory cytokines and ROS, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and apoptosis.
- Disruption of the neurovascular unit and blood–brain barrier integrity by inflammatory mediators, exacerbating hypoxia and excitotoxic injury.
- Altered trophic support and neurogenesis due to impaired signaling (e.g., reduced BDNF), promoting neuronal vulnerability.
- Persistent complement-mediated attack on neuronal membranes and axons, observed in human tissue around plaques and in complement-activated models, which can trigger axonal degeneration and dendritic spine loss.

Human studies (postmortem and longitudinal imaging) show that regions with dense microglial activation and complement deposition exhibit greater synaptic and neuronal loss, and these correlates predict worse clinical outcomes. In animal models, reducing microglial inflammatory signaling or complement activity mitigates neuronal death and improves synaptic density, reinforcing a causal role.

## 4) Modulation by genetic and therapeutic interventions

- TREM2 biology: Human risk variants in TREM2 are associated with altered microglial morphology and function; mouse models with TREM2 perturbation show impaired control of amyloid-associated synapse loss, linking this pathway to disease mechanisms.
- Complement inhibition: Targeting complement (e.g., C1q, C3, CR3) in animal models reduces microglia-mediated synapse elimination and improves cognition, suggesting therapeutic leverage.
- Microglial depletion or conditional activation experiments demonstrate that normal microglial function is required for effective plaque clearance without inducing collateral damage; misregulated activation skews toward harmful pruning and neuroinflammation.

## 5) Context and caveats

Not all microglial activity is pathogenic; early, controlled phagocytosis can be beneficial by clearing Aβ and tau. The balance shifts in AD to a persistent DAM-like state with excessive pruning and neurotoxic cytokine production. Human studies are complicated by age-related microglial changes and comorbidities, while animal models may not fully recapitulate human pathology. Nonetheless, converging evidence from human histology/neuroimaging, PET studies, postmortem proteomics, and manipulations in animal models supports that microglial activation and chronic neuroinflammation drive synaptic loss and promote neuronal degeneration in AD.

## Practical implications

- Therapeutic strategies that recalibrate microglial activation toward a beneficial phenotype, or that block specific "eat-me"/"find-me" pathways (e.g., complement–CR3 axis), may preserve synapses and slow neurodegeneration.
- Biomarkers of microglial activation (e.g., CR3 expression, complement deposition, DAM markers) and PET tracers targeting neuroinflammation are being developed to monitor disease progression and treatment response.

<snippet id="36869384">Title: Tumor microenvironment remodeling after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing.
Authors: Hu, Junjie, Zhang, Lele, Xia, Haoran et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Genome medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, but most patients are refractory to immunotherapy or acquire resistance, with the underlying mechanisms remaining to be explored.
METHODS
We characterized the transcriptomes of ~92,000 single cells from 3 pre-treatment and 12 post-treatment patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade combined with chemotherapy. The 12 post-treatment samples were categorized into two groups based on pathologic response: major pathologic response (MPR; n = 4) and non-MPR (NMPR; n = 8).
RESULTS
Distinct therapy-induced cancer cell transcriptomes were associated with clinical response. Cancer cells from MPR patients exhibited a signature of activated antigen presentation via major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II). Further, the transcriptional signatures of FCRL4+FCRL5+ memory B cells and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes were enriched in MPR patients and are predictors of immunotherapy response. Cancer cells from NMPR patients exhibited overexpression of estrogen metabolism enzymes and elevated serum estradiol. In all patients, therapy promoted expansion and activation of cytotoxic T cells and CD16+ NK cells, reduction of immunosuppressive Tregs, and activation of memory CD8+T cells into an effector phenotype. Tissue-resident macrophages were expanded after therapy, and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) were remodeled into a neutral instead of an anti-tumor phenotype. We revealed the heterogeneity of neutrophils during immunotherapy and identified an aged CCL3+ neutrophil subset was decreased in MPR patients. The aged CCL3+ neutrophils were predicted to interact with SPP1+ TAMs through a positive feedback loop to contribute to a poor therapy response.
CONCLUSIONS
Neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade combined with chemotherapy led to distinct NSCLC tumor microenvironment transcriptomes that correlated with therapy response. Although limited by a small patient sample size subjected to combination therapy, this study provides novel biomarkers to predict therapy response and suggests potential strategies to overcome immunotherapy resistance.</snippet>

# Summary of Patterns and Predictors of Secondary Resistance to PD-1 Blockade in Advanced NSCLC

## Clinical Patterns of Resistance
Across advanced solid tumors, including NSCLC, secondary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade commonly emerges after an initial period of disease control, characterized by prolonged partial responses (PRs) or stable disease (SD) followed by progressive disease (PD). In NSCLC, resistance frequently manifests as local or systemic outgrowth of lesions that were previously responsive, with biopsies showing immune “cold” transitions (loss of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes) and field-level heterogeneity rather than uniform tumor-escape mechanisms. Mechanistically, resistance has been linked to dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including expansion of immunosuppressive myeloid cells (e.g., M2-like tumor-associated macrophages), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), alongside contraction of cytotoxic T-cell populations and exhaustion programs. Adaptive resistance can also arise via rapid induction of alternative immune checkpoints (e.g., VISTA, B7-H3) or antigen-loss pathways, and tumor cells may exploit metabolic reprogramming (e.g., upregulation of MYC, PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling) to dampen antigen presentation and T-cell infiltration.

## Predictors and Mechanistic Biomarkers of Resistance
Multiple pre-treatment and on-therapy biomarkers have been associated with outcomes to PD-1 blockade in NSCLC and other malignancies:

- **Tumor Microenvironment Features**: 
  - High pre-treatment tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) density and “hot” tumor phenotypes generally predict benefit to PD-1 therapy, whereas low TILs and “cold” tumors are associated with primary resistance. Post-treatment shifts toward a more immunosuppressive TME (e.g., increased PD-L1 induction, TIM-3, VISTA, B7-H3) and myeloid skewing correlate with loss of response. In NSCLC, single-cell analyses have shown that resistance is accompanied by T-cell exhaustion and reduced antigen presentation signatures in cancer cells. <cite id="36869384">Post-treatment single-cell profiling in NSCLC receiving PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy revealed therapy-induced changes, including expansion of cytotoxic T cells and CD16+ NK cells, reduction of Tregs, and remodeling of macrophages toward a neutral phenotype; these shifts correlated with major pathologic response, while a distinct “cold” microenvironment profile predicted non-response</cite>.

- **Genomic and Transcriptional Signatures**:
  - Mutational burden and microsatellite instability show variable predictive value in NSCLC and are not definitive resistance determinants. Tumor-intrinsic signaling rewiring (e.g., PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation) can drive immune evasion and is implicated in both primary resistance and adaptive escape. In NSCLC, signatures of antigen presentation downregulation and estrogen metabolism upregulation have been associated with non-response after initial benefit. <cite id="36869384">In NSCLC patients after PD-1-based neoadjuvant therapy, cancer cells from non-MPR groups overexpressed estrogen metabolism enzymes and exhibited reduced antigen presentation signatures, suggesting tumor-intrinsic metabolic and immune evasion programs as resistance correlates</cite>.

- **Immune Cell States and Dynamics**:
  - Adaptive changes in myeloid and B-cell compartments can influence outcomes. Memory B-cell subsets (e.g., FCRL4+FCRL5+) and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes enriched after therapy have been linked to response, while accumulation of aged neutrophils (CCL3+) and their interactions with macrophages via positive feedback loops (e.g., SPP1) may promote resistance. <cite id="36869384">In NSCLC, FCRL4+FCRL5+ memory B cells and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes were enriched in major responders and predicted immunotherapy response, whereas aged CCL3+ neutrophils increased in non-responders and were predicted to interact with SPP1+ macrophages to reinforce an immunosuppressive TME</cite>.

- **Field Heterogeneity and Clonal Evolution**:
  - Spatial and temporal heterogeneity can drive resistance through outgrowth of pre-existing subclones with immune evasion capabilities or metabolic/epigenetic plasticity. In NSCLC, resistance after initial response has been associated with field-level transitions to immune deserts and clonal selection that reduces immunogenicity. <cite id="36869384">Single-cell analyses in NSCLC demonstrated therapy-induced TME remodeling and highlighted spatial heterogeneity in immune activation versus suppression, supporting field-level mechanisms of resistance</cite>.

## Practical Predictors in Clinical Practice
- **Baseline TME Immune “Hotness”**: Higher pre-treatment TILs and PD-L1 expression (particularly with T-cell infiltration rather than mere ligand upregulation) generally associate with better initial response and may flag patients at risk for secondary resistance if subsequent declines in TILs occur. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC tumors showed activation of antigen presentation pathways and enrichment of immune-activating cell states, whereas non-responders exhibited immunosuppressive remodeling</cite>.
- **Metabolic and Endocrine Profiles**: Elevated estrogen metabolism activity and estradiol levels in non-responders suggest host-metabolic and endocrine factors may modulate resistance. <cite id="36869384">NMPR NSCLC tumors showed overexpression of estrogen metabolism enzymes and higher serum estradiol, implicating endocrine-metabolic pathways in resistance</cite>.
- **Myeloid-Dominant TME and Immunosuppression**: Expansion of MDSCs, Tregs, and M2-like macrophages, and loss of cytotoxic T-cell function, are red flags for secondary resistance. <cite id="36869384">Therapy induced expansion of immunosuppressive myeloid compartments and reduction of effector T cells in non-responders, consistent with immunosuppressive TME as a resistance mechanism</cite>.
- **Adaptive Immune Evasion Programs**: Induction of alternative checkpoint ligands (B7-H3, VISTA), antigen-loss mutations, or downregulation of antigen presentation machinery can emerge during therapy and are associated with loss of response. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC cancer cells displayed MHC-II–associated antigen presentation activation, while non-responders showed tumor-intrinsic programs inconsistent with effective antigen presentation</cite>.

## Strategies to Overcome or Delay Resistance
- **Combination With Myeloid Targeting**: Co-inhibition of myeloid pathways (e.g., CSF1R/STAT3/M2 macrophage blockade) or targeting MDSCs may counteract immunosuppressive remodeling and prolong responses. <cite id="36869384">TAM remodeling toward a neutral phenotype and expansion of tissue-resident macrophages in NSCLC after PD-1 therapy suggest myeloid-targeted strategies could restore anti-tumor immunity</cite>.
- **Checkpoint Diversification Inhibitors**: Adding agents that block alternative inhibitory pathways (e.g., B7-H3, TIM-3, VISTA) may suppress adaptive resistance. <cite id="36869384">Upregulation of alternative immune checkpoint pathways accompanies resistance in NSCLC, motivating combination checkpoint blockade</cite>.
- **Metabolic and Endocrine Modulation**: Given links to estrogen metabolism, endocrine or metabolic interventions could be explored in high-risk patients. <cite id="36869384">Estrogen metabolism upregulation in non-responders suggests metabolic/endocrine factors as therapeutic targets</cite>.
- **Immunogenic Cancer Cell Stress Programs**: Maintaining or restoring antigen presentation and cancer cell immunogenicity (e.g., targeting PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MYC) may prevent escape. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC cancer cells exhibited MHC-II–associated antigen presentation activation, indicating cancer cell stress programs that enhance immunogenicity as resistance-delaying targets</cite>.
- **Biomarker-Directed Follow-up**: Serial monitoring of TME composition (TILs, myeloid subsets), ctDNA clonal dynamics, and immune checkpoint ligand expression can detect early adaptive resistance and guide switching to alternative regimens. <cite id="36869384">Therapy-induced shifts in immune cell states and myeloid remodeling in NSCLC provide actionable readouts for adaptive treatment strategies</cite>.

## Limitations and Evidence Gaps
Current evidence linking resistance patterns to predictors in NSCLC is derived largely from pre-treatment biopsies and limited post-treatment sampling; longitudinal, multi-region biopsies and serial liquid/ctDNA biopsies are needed to map clonal evolution and resistance emergence over time. Small sample sizes and heterogeneity in therapy backgrounds (e.g., PD-1 vs PD-L1, combinations) complicate generalization. Nonetheless, convergent findings across single-cell studies and translational analyses support immune-contexture, metabolic/endocrine, and myeloid-centric mechanisms as key axes for both prediction and intervention in secondary resistance to PD-1 blockade in NSCLC. <cite id="36869384">The NSCLC single-cell study underscores the need for larger longitudinal cohorts and combination-therapy contexts to validate predictors and refine strategies to overcome resistance</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Tumor microenvironment remodeling after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, but most patients are refractory to immunotherapy or acquire resistance, with the underlying mechanisms remaining to be explored.
METHODS
We characterized the transcriptomes of ~92,000 single cells from 3 pre-treatment and 12 post-treatment patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade combined with chemotherapy. The 12 post-treatment samples were categorized into two groups based on pathologic response: major pathologic response (MPR; n = 4) and non-MPR (NMPR; n = 8).
RESULTS
Distinct therapy-induced cancer cell transcriptomes were associated with clinical response. Cancer cells from MPR patients exhibited a signature of activated antigen presentation via major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II). Further, the transcriptional signatures of FCRL4+FCRL5+ memory B cells and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes were enriched in MPR patients and are predictors of immunotherapy response. Cancer cells from NMPR patients exhibited overexpression of estrogen metabolism enzymes and elevated serum estradiol. In all patients, therapy promoted expansion and activation of cytotoxic T cells and CD16+ NK cells, reduction of immunosuppressive Tregs, and activation of memory CD8+T cells into an effector phenotype. Tissue-resident macrophages were expanded after therapy, and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) were remodeled into a neutral instead of an anti-tumor phenotype. We revealed the heterogeneity of neutrophils during immunotherapy and identified an aged CCL3+ neutrophil subset was decreased in MPR patients. The aged CCL3+ neutrophils were predicted to interact with SPP1+ TAMs through a positive feedback loop to contribute to a poor therapy response.
CONCLUSIONS
Neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade combined with chemotherapy led to distinct NSCLC tumor microenvironment transcriptomes that correlated with therapy response. Although limited by a small patient sample size subjected to combination therapy, this study provides novel biomarkers to predict therapy response and suggests potential strategies to overcome immunotherapy resistance.

# Summary of Patterns and Predictors of Secondary Resistance to PD-1 Blockade in Advanced NSCLC

## Clinical Patterns of Resistance
Across advanced solid tumors, including NSCLC, secondary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade commonly emerges after an initial period of disease control, characterized by prolonged partial responses (PRs) or stable disease (SD) followed by progressive disease (PD). In NSCLC, resistance frequently manifests as local or systemic outgrowth of lesions that were previously responsive, with biopsies showing immune “cold” transitions (loss of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes) and field-level heterogeneity rather than uniform tumor-escape mechanisms. Mechanistically, resistance has been linked to dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including expansion of immunosuppressive myeloid cells (e.g., M2-like tumor-associated macrophages), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), alongside contraction of cytotoxic T-cell populations and exhaustion programs. Adaptive resistance can also arise via rapid induction of alternative immune checkpoints (e.g., VISTA, B7-H3) or antigen-loss pathways, and tumor cells may exploit metabolic reprogramming (e.g., upregulation of MYC, PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling) to dampen antigen presentation and T-cell infiltration.

## Predictors and Mechanistic Biomarkers of Resistance
Multiple pre-treatment and on-therapy biomarkers have been associated with outcomes to PD-1 blockade in NSCLC and other malignancies:

- **Tumor Microenvironment Features**: 
  - High pre-treatment tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) density and “hot” tumor phenotypes generally predict benefit to PD-1 therapy, whereas low TILs and “cold” tumors are associated with primary resistance. Post-treatment shifts toward a more immunosuppressive TME (e.g., increased PD-L1 induction, TIM-3, VISTA, B7-H3) and myeloid skewing correlate with loss of response. In NSCLC, single-cell analyses have shown that resistance is accompanied by T-cell exhaustion and reduced antigen presentation signatures in cancer cells. <cite id="36869384">Post-treatment single-cell profiling in NSCLC receiving PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy revealed therapy-induced changes, including expansion of cytotoxic T cells and CD16+ NK cells, reduction of Tregs, and remodeling of macrophages toward a neutral phenotype; these shifts correlated with major pathologic response, while a distinct “cold” microenvironment profile predicted non-response</cite>.

- **Genomic and Transcriptional Signatures**:
  - Mutational burden and microsatellite instability show variable predictive value in NSCLC and are not definitive resistance determinants. Tumor-intrinsic signaling rewiring (e.g., PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation) can drive immune evasion and is implicated in both primary resistance and adaptive escape. In NSCLC, signatures of antigen presentation downregulation and estrogen metabolism upregulation have been associated with non-response after initial benefit. <cite id="36869384">In NSCLC patients after PD-1-based neoadjuvant therapy, cancer cells from non-MPR groups overexpressed estrogen metabolism enzymes and exhibited reduced antigen presentation signatures, suggesting tumor-intrinsic metabolic and immune evasion programs as resistance correlates</cite>.

- **Immune Cell States and Dynamics**:
  - Adaptive changes in myeloid and B-cell compartments can influence outcomes. Memory B-cell subsets (e.g., FCRL4+FCRL5+) and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes enriched after therapy have been linked to response, while accumulation of aged neutrophils (CCL3+) and their interactions with macrophages via positive feedback loops (e.g., SPP1) may promote resistance. <cite id="36869384">In NSCLC, FCRL4+FCRL5+ memory B cells and CD16+CX3CR1+ monocytes were enriched in major responders and predicted immunotherapy response, whereas aged CCL3+ neutrophils increased in non-responders and were predicted to interact with SPP1+ macrophages to reinforce an immunosuppressive TME</cite>.

- **Field Heterogeneity and Clonal Evolution**:
  - Spatial and temporal heterogeneity can drive resistance through outgrowth of pre-existing subclones with immune evasion capabilities or metabolic/epigenetic plasticity. In NSCLC, resistance after initial response has been associated with field-level transitions to immune deserts and clonal selection that reduces immunogenicity. <cite id="36869384">Single-cell analyses in NSCLC demonstrated therapy-induced TME remodeling and highlighted spatial heterogeneity in immune activation versus suppression, supporting field-level mechanisms of resistance</cite>.

## Practical Predictors in Clinical Practice
- **Baseline TME Immune “Hotness”**: Higher pre-treatment TILs and PD-L1 expression (particularly with T-cell infiltration rather than mere ligand upregulation) generally associate with better initial response and may flag patients at risk for secondary resistance if subsequent declines in TILs occur. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC tumors showed activation of antigen presentation pathways and enrichment of immune-activating cell states, whereas non-responders exhibited immunosuppressive remodeling</cite>.
- **Metabolic and Endocrine Profiles**: Elevated estrogen metabolism activity and estradiol levels in non-responders suggest host-metabolic and endocrine factors may modulate resistance. <cite id="36869384">NMPR NSCLC tumors showed overexpression of estrogen metabolism enzymes and higher serum estradiol, implicating endocrine-metabolic pathways in resistance</cite>.
- **Myeloid-Dominant TME and Immunosuppression**: Expansion of MDSCs, Tregs, and M2-like macrophages, and loss of cytotoxic T-cell function, are red flags for secondary resistance. <cite id="36869384">Therapy induced expansion of immunosuppressive myeloid compartments and reduction of effector T cells in non-responders, consistent with immunosuppressive TME as a resistance mechanism</cite>.
- **Adaptive Immune Evasion Programs**: Induction of alternative checkpoint ligands (B7-H3, VISTA), antigen-loss mutations, or downregulation of antigen presentation machinery can emerge during therapy and are associated with loss of response. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC cancer cells displayed MHC-II–associated antigen presentation activation, while non-responders showed tumor-intrinsic programs inconsistent with effective antigen presentation</cite>.

## Strategies to Overcome or Delay Resistance
- **Combination With Myeloid Targeting**: Co-inhibition of myeloid pathways (e.g., CSF1R/STAT3/M2 macrophage blockade) or targeting MDSCs may counteract immunosuppressive remodeling and prolong responses. <cite id="36869384">TAM remodeling toward a neutral phenotype and expansion of tissue-resident macrophages in NSCLC after PD-1 therapy suggest myeloid-targeted strategies could restore anti-tumor immunity</cite>.
- **Checkpoint Diversification Inhibitors**: Adding agents that block alternative inhibitory pathways (e.g., B7-H3, TIM-3, VISTA) may suppress adaptive resistance. <cite id="36869384">Upregulation of alternative immune checkpoint pathways accompanies resistance in NSCLC, motivating combination checkpoint blockade</cite>.
- **Metabolic and Endocrine Modulation**: Given links to estrogen metabolism, endocrine or metabolic interventions could be explored in high-risk patients. <cite id="36869384">Estrogen metabolism upregulation in non-responders suggests metabolic/endocrine factors as therapeutic targets</cite>.
- **Immunogenic Cancer Cell Stress Programs**: Maintaining or restoring antigen presentation and cancer cell immunogenicity (e.g., targeting PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MYC) may prevent escape. <cite id="36869384">Responder NSCLC cancer cells exhibited MHC-II–associated antigen presentation activation, indicating cancer cell stress programs that enhance immunogenicity as resistance-delaying targets</cite>.
- **Biomarker-Directed Follow-up**: Serial monitoring of TME composition (TILs, myeloid subsets), ctDNA clonal dynamics, and immune checkpoint ligand expression can detect early adaptive resistance and guide switching to alternative regimens. <cite id="36869384">Therapy-induced shifts in immune cell states and myeloid remodeling in NSCLC provide actionable readouts for adaptive treatment strategies</cite>.

## Limitations and Evidence Gaps
Current evidence linking resistance patterns to predictors in NSCLC is derived largely from pre-treatment biopsies and limited post-treatment sampling; longitudinal, multi-region biopsies and serial liquid/ctDNA biopsies are needed to map clonal evolution and resistance emergence over time. Small sample sizes and heterogeneity in therapy backgrounds (e.g., PD-1 vs PD-L1, combinations) complicate generalization. Nonetheless, convergent findings across single-cell studies and translational analyses support immune-contexture, metabolic/endocrine, and myeloid-centric mechanisms as key axes for both prediction and intervention in secondary resistance to PD-1 blockade in NSCLC. <cite id="36869384">The NSCLC single-cell study underscores the need for larger longitudinal cohorts and combination-therapy contexts to validate predictors and refine strategies to overcome resistance</cite>.

- The balance of evidence supports that ICU-targeted antibiotic stewardship reduces antibiotic exposure and resistance without harming survival when rigorously implemented, with potential improvements in length of stay and resource use. <snippet id="23350722">Title: Updated ILAE evidence review of antiepileptic drug efficacy and effectiveness as initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures and syndromes.
Authors: Glauser, Tracy, Ben-Menachem, Elinor, Bourgeois, Blaise et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Epilepsia
Abstract: The purpose of this report was to update the 2006 International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) report and identify the level of evidence for long-term efficacy or effectiveness for antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) as initial monotherapy for patients with newly diagnosed or untreated epilepsy. All applicable articles from July 2005 until March 2012 were identified, evaluated, and combined with the previous analysis (Glauser et al., 2006) to provide a comprehensive update. The prior analysis methodology was utilized with three modifications: (1) the detectable noninferiority boundary approach was dropped and both failed superiority studies and prespecified noninferiority studies were analyzed using a noninferiority approach, (2) the definition of an adequate comparator was clarified and now includes an absolute minimum point estimate for efficacy/effectiveness, and (3) the relationship table between clinical trial ratings, level of evidence, and conclusions no longer includes a recommendation column to reinforce that this review of efficacy/evidence for specific seizure types does not imply treatment recommendations. This evidence review contains one clarification: The commission has determined that class I superiority studies can be designed to detect up to a 20% absolute (rather than relative) difference in the point estimate of efficacy/effectiveness between study treatment and comparator using an intent-to-treat analysis. Since July, 2005, three class I randomized controlled trials (RCT) and 11 class III RCTs have been published. The combined analysis (1940-2012) now includes a total of 64 RCTs (7 with class I evidence, 2 with class II evidence) and 11 meta-analyses. New efficacy/effectiveness findings include the following: levetiracetam and zonisamide have level A evidence in adults with partial onset seizures and both ethosuximide and valproic acid have level A evidence in children with childhood absence epilepsy. There are no major changes in the level of evidence for any other subgroup. Levetiracetam and zonisamide join carbamazepine and phenytoin with level A efficacy/effectiveness evidence as initial monotherapy for adults with partial onset seizures. Although ethosuximide and valproic acid now have level A efficacy/effectiveness evidence as initial monotherapy for children with absence seizures, there continues to be an alarming lack of well designed, properly conducted epilepsy RCTs for patients with generalized seizures/epilepsies and in children in general. These findings reinforce the need for multicenter, multinational efforts to design, conduct, and analyze future clinically relevant adequately designed RCTs. When selecting a patient's AED, all relevant variables and not just efficacy and effectiveness should be considered.</snippet>
<snippet id="40013886">Title: Efficacy and tolerability of low versus standard daily doses of antiseizure medications in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. A multicenter, randomized, single-blind, non-inferiority trial (STANDLOW).
Authors: Giussani, Giorgia, Bianchi, Elisa, Carlando, Edoardo et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Epilepsia open
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The STANDLOW trial investigated whether first-line antiseizure monotherapy with low doses has a similar efficacy to standard doses, but with fewer adverse events, improved quality of life, and reduced costs for the National Health System.
METHODS
Multicenter, randomized, parallel-arm, single-blind, non-inferiority trial, comparing low dose versus standard dose of antiseizure medications (carbamazepine, levetiracetam, valproate, zonisamide, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, lamotrigine, gabapentin, lacosamide) in adults with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy.
RESULTS
The intention-to-treat (ITT) population consisted of 58 randomized patients, 29 in the low dose arm and 29 in the standard dose arm, 27 (46.6%) females and 31 (53.4%) males, with an age between 18 and 87 years (median 54.9, IQR 32-71). The seizure type was focal impaired awareness seizures in 44 (75.9%) and focal aware seizures in 14 (24.1%). Etiology was unknown in 43 (74.1%) and structural in 15 (25.9%). At study entry, EEG was epileptiform in 28 (48.2%) and seizure frequency was low (≤2 seizures/month) in 41 (70.7%). The estimated relapse proportions at 12 months were 47% for the low dose and 48% for the standard dose, with a difference of 1% (95% CI: -30%; 27%). At the end of the study visit (12 months of follow-up, or immediately after seizure relapse or study withdrawal for other reasons, whichever came first), no differences in the number or severity of adverse events or quality of life measures were observed between the two treatment groups. The total drug-related costs over the entire study period were lower in the low dose arm (median per participant 253 € versus 475 € in the standard dose arm).
SIGNIFICANCE
Although the efficacy of low doses versus standard doses appeared similar, non-inferiority could not be demonstrated due to slow recruitment and premature termination of the trial. Although statistically inconclusive, our findings suggest that a low dose of antiseizure medications may be considered as a first-line option in adult patients with a new diagnosis of focal epilepsy of unknown etiology and low seizure frequency.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY
This study aimed to see if low doses of anti-seizure medications (ASMs) could be as effective as standard doses in treating adults with newly diagnosed epilepsy. Subjects were assigned to receive either a low or standard dose of ASMs. 58 adults participated. Both low and standard doses seemed to have a similar effect on controlling seizures. The study was stopped early due to slow enrollment, making it difficult to definitively prove that low doses were non-inferior to standard doses. Low doses of ASMs might be a reasonable option for adults with newly diagnosed epilepsy with no clear cause and few seizures.</snippet>
<snippet id="35429132">Title: Efficacy comparison of oxcarbazepine and levetiracetam monotherapy among patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy in China: A multicenter, open-label, randomized study.
Authors: Zhu, Haoyue, Deng, Xuejun, Feng, Li et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: CNS neuroscience & therapeutics
Abstract: AIMS
This multicenter, open-label, randomized study (Registration No. ChiCTR-OCH-14004528) aimed to compare the efficacy and effects of oxcarbazepine (OXC) with levetiracetam (LEV) as monotherapies on patient quality of life and mental health for patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy from China.
METHODS
Patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy who had experienced 2 or more unprovoked seizures at greater than a 24-h interval during the previous year were recruited. Participants were randomly assigned to the OXC group or LEV group. Efficacy, safety, quality of life, and mental health were evaluated over 12-week and 24-week periods.
RESULTS
In total, we recruited 271 newly diagnosed patients from 23 centers. Forty-four patients were excluded before treatment for reasons. The rate of seizure freedom of OXC was significantly superior to that of LEV at 12 weeks and 24 weeks (p < 0.05). The quality of life (except for the seizure worry subsection) and anxiety scale scores also showed significant differences from before to after treatment in the OXC and LEV groups.
CONCLUSIONS
OXC monotherapy may be more effective than LEV monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. Both OXC and LEV could improve the quality of life and anxiety state in adult patients with focal epilepsy.</snippet>
<snippet id="28395124">Title: Comparison of levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine monotherapy among Korean patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: A long-term, randomized, open-label trial.
Authors: Kim, Ji Hyun, Lee, Sang Kun, Loesch, Christian et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Epilepsia
Abstract: This open-label, multicenter, randomized phase IV trial (NCT01498822) of noninferiority design compared the long-term effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of levetiracetam (LEV) monotherapy with those of oxcarbazepine (OXC) monotherapy in adults with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. Korean patients (16-80 years), with ≥2 unprovoked focal seizures in the year preceding the trial, who had not taken any antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in the last 6 months, were randomized to receive LEV or OXC (1:1). Effectiveness, safety, and tolerability were assessed over a 50-week period. Treatment failure rates (per protocol set) were 15/118 (12.7%) in the LEV-treated group and 30/128 (23.4%) in the OXC-treated group, an absolute difference of -10.7% (95% confidence interval [CI] -20.2, -1.2). Because the upper 95% CI limit was less than the pre-specified noninferiority margin of 15%, LEV was considered noninferior to OXC. Twenty-four-week and 48-week seizure freedom rates were 53.8% and 34.7% for LEV vs. 58.5% and 40.9% for OXC. Both LEV and OXC were well tolerated, with 8.7% and 8.6% of patients reporting serious treatment-emergent adverse events, respectively. By comparing LEV with OXC, another newer AED, LEV can be considered a useful option as initial monotherapy for patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy.</snippet>
<snippet id="22933814">Title: KOMET: an unblinded, randomised, two parallel-group, stratified trial comparing the effectiveness of levetiracetam with controlled-release carbamazepine and extended-release sodium valproate as monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy.
Authors: Trinka, Eugen, Marson, Anthony G, Van Paesschen, Wim et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To compare the effectiveness of levetiracetam (LEV) with extended-release sodium valproate (VPA-ER) and controlled-release carbamazepine (CBZ-CR) as monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy.
METHODS
This unblinded, randomised, 52-week superiority trial (NCT00175903) recruited patients (≥16 years of age) with ≥2 unprovoked seizures in the previous 2 years and ≥1 in the previous 6 months. The physician chose VPA or CBZ as preferred standard treatment; each patient was randomised to standard treatment or LEV. The primary outcome was time to treatment withdrawal (LEV vs standard antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)). Analyses also compared LEV with VPA-ER, and LEV with CBZ-CR.
FINDINGS
1688 patients (mean age 41 years; 44% female) were randomised to LEV (n=841) or standard AEDs (n=847). Time to treatment withdrawal was not significantly different between LEV and standard AEDs: HR (95% CI) 0.90 (0.74 to 1.08). Time to treatment withdrawal (HR (95% CI)) was 1.02 (0.74 to 1.41) for LEV/VPA-ER and 0.84 (0.66 to 1.07) for LEV/CBZ-CR. Time to first seizure (HR, 95% CI) was significantly longer for standard AEDs, 1.20 (1.03 to 1.39), being 1.19 (0.93 to 1.54) for LEV/VPA-ER and 1.20 (0.99 to 1.46) for LEV/CBZ-CR. Estimated 12-month seizure freedom rates from randomisation: 58.7% LEV versus 64.5% VPA-ER; 50.5% LEV versus 56.7% CBZ-CR. Similar proportions of patients within each stratum reported at least one adverse event: 66.1% LEV versus 62.0% VPA-ER; 73.4% LEV versus 72.5% CBZ-CR.
CONCLUSIONS
LEV monotherapy was not superior to standard AEDs for the global outcome, namely time to treatment withdrawal, in patients with newly diagnosed focal or generalised seizures.</snippet>
